sources.title: Apple is reportedly building a smart home camera that won't record video footage of you or anyone else - Engadget
passages: Gurman added that the security camera will use "a very similar technology to what they're going to be using for the AirPods with cameras," which leaked over the summer.

Based on code buried in an early build of macOS Tahoe 26.7, these AirPods will each have their own tiny embedded cameras that take extremely low resolution RGB still images that can be analyzed using Visual Intelligence.
In the wake of Meta's "pervert glasses" fallout, Apple's camera-equipped AirPods reportedly won't be able to take pictures or record video.
The Bloomberg reporter says the camera device is a companion product to Apple's also as-yet unannounced smart home display, which the company is referring to internally as J490.
These small cameras can be installed around your home and will apparently be cylindrical, resembling chapstick.
Gurman says they will have a very low frame rate and crucially won't actually offer video recording as a feature.
If the camera identifies someone walking into a room, it can notify you of whether you know that person or not, but you'll only receive text descriptions.

As well as the home hub device, which will be the centrepiece of the whole Siri-led smart home push, Gurman claims that Apple will also launch more powerful versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV, which will both support the new Siri AI ecosystem.
What's the point of a camera that doesn't capture moving images, you may ask?

Apple appears to be mindful of the growing and very reasonable concerns about over-surveillance and what happens with that data, and so the sensor will instead use AI to analyze movement in your home.

After finally making Siri a half-decent assistant in this year's round of major OS updates, it looks like the smart home is going to Apple's big area of focus in the coming months. Reliable Apple insider Mark Gurman revealed earlier this week that the company's long-awaited home hub could arrive later in October, and in the debut episode of his new Power On podcast, he predicted that a security camera may follow. But unlike its many soon-to-be rivals, this one somewhat bizarrely won't actually record video. As well as the home hub device, which will be the centrepiece of the whole Siri-led smart home push, Gurman claims that Apple will also launch more powerful versions of the HomePod mini and Apple TV, which will both support the new Siri AI ecosystem. But the camera is arguably more interesting, as much for what it can't do as what it can. Apple appears to be mindful of the growing and very reasonable concerns about over-surveillance and what happens with that data, and so the sensor will instead use AI to analyze movement in your home. passages: New Apple products are reportedly launching October 13, including the rumored ‘HomePad’ device.

Today Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple plans to announce three new Home products very soon.
Apple aims to eventually update its larger HomePod speaker as well.

For two years he co-hosted the Adapt podcast on Relay FM, which focused entirely on the iPad.
As a result, it should come as no surprise that his favorite Apple device is the iPad Pro.

sources.title: How Apple can win the smart home
passages: Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously.
According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV.
This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event.

Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home.

Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls.

Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home.
Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems.

While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware.
The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014.
Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands.
Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation.

extraction.body: This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event. While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware. Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously. According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV. The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014. As exciting as this is (and I’ll be there in person to check it out), the real shift will be bringing Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into the home. Apple is years behind Google and Amazon in smart-home hardware, but success in the home depends far more on software. That’s where Apple could leapfrog the competition. Apple announced the HomePod Mini on October 13th, 2020, six years to the day from this week’s event, and the newest Apple TV 4K is now four years old. And those aren’t dedicated smart home devices; they’re more content-consumption gadgets with a side of home automation. Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls. Based on leaks, Apple’s product doesn’t sound that different from what’s come before. According to Bloomberg, it will have a 6-inch square display on a speaker base or as a wall-mounted option, facial recognition to show your personal messages and calendar, a minimalist touchscreen interface to control locks and thermostats, and FaceTime and intercom calls. The difference has to be in the software and the smart assistant that powers it. Bloomberg reports the smart display will launch with a brand-new homeOS built around Siri AI. Generative AI has breathed new life into the smart home voice assistant by both making it easier to talk to and expanding its capabilities. Until now, Apple’s new Siri AI has been MIA from its HomePods and Apple TV; when you talk to those, the old Siri responds in its basic, functional way. [Image: Apple’s smart speakers: the HomePod and HomePod Mini. Amazon and Google launched theirs last year, but Alexa Plus is only just starting to get it right, and Google’s Gemini for Home, an underpowered version of Gemini, is a confusing mess of capabilities. Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands. So far, every company has hit significant roadblocks bringing a smarter assistant to the home. Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home. These cautious approaches are down to the fact that the home is a big, complicated, messy, multi-user environment that is hard to control. An agentic AI getting something wrong could have consequences far greater than accidentally sending an email. Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems. Every home is different, with unique needs — there is no single plug-and-play solution. Progress has been made toward solving one of the smart home’s biggest challenges: interoperability, with open standards like Matter and Thread promising to make setting up and using a smart home easier. It’s the platforms that have to make the smart home work. Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation. That’s where Siri AI and Apple Intelligence could play a major role. While Apple used Gemini models to build Siri AI, Google itself has struggled to deliver a compelling experience in the home. Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home. This will be the next level for the smart home; with reliable data and context, your home could know who’s in it, where they are, and what they need, and, combined with knowing the status of every device, become proactive. For example, it could alert you that the oven is on and no one is home, suggest turning off the AC when a window is left open, and route messages and notifications to the room you’re in. Today, Apple Home has significant limitations: it doesn’t support every type of home device (no fridges, washing machines, or EV chargers); it can’t control every feature of many device types; and its automations are limited compared to the competition (notably lacking conditional programming options inside the app). All this makes the Home app very easy to use, but extremely underpowered. With Siri AI, Apple could unlock many of those capabilities via voice instead of building complicated menu interfaces.

sources.title: Apple is working with LG on new smart home products, here are the details - GSMArena.com news - GSMArena.com
passages: According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, a very reliable source of Apple-related information, Apple is working with LG on a range of new smart home products.

That said, we're not exactly sure what Apple's involvement will actually be, since these will allegedly be called LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat, and LG Temperature Sensor.
LG has recently sought regulatory approval for these products from the FCC and UL Solutions.
Gurman says LG is handling the manufacturing and product support, even though Apple was (somehow) involved in the development.
Apple has done similar things in the past, working with Belkin and Logitech on accessories.
Such an arrangement gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem "without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories", as Gurman puts it.
Apple can also help "shape the products' design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps".

coreStoryFacts.text: Gurman added that the security camera will use "a very similar technology to what they're going to be using for the AirPods with cameras," which leaked over the summer.

In the wake of Meta's "pervert glasses" fallout, Apple's camera-equipped AirPods reportedly won't be able to take pictures or record video.
The Bloomberg reporter says the camera device is a companion product to Apple's also as-yet unannounced smart home display, which the company is referring to internally as J490.
These small cameras can be installed around your home and will apparently be cylindrical, resembling chapstick.

What's the point of a camera that doesn't capture moving images, you may ask?

Apple appears to be mindful of the growing and very reasonable concerns about over-surveillance and what happens with that data, and so the sensor will instead use AI to analyze movement in your home.

After finally making Siri a half-decent assistant in this year's round of major OS updates, it looks like the smart home is going to Apple's big area of focus in the coming months. sources.title: How Apple can win the smart home
passages: Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously.
According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV.
This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event.

Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home.

Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls.

Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home.
Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems.

While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware.
The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014.
Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands.
Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation.

extraction.body: This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event. While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware. Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously. According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV. The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014. As exciting as this is (and I’ll be there in person to check it out), the real shift will be bringing Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into the home. Apple is years behind Google and Amazon in smart-home hardware, but success in the home depends far more on software. That’s where Apple could leapfrog the competition. Apple announced the HomePod Mini on October 13th, 2020, six years to the day from this week’s event, and the newest Apple TV 4K is now four years old. And those aren’t dedicated smart home devices; they’re more content-consumption gadgets with a side of home automation. Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls. Based on leaks, Apple’s product doesn’t sound that different from what’s come before. According to Bloomberg, it will have a 6-inch square display on a speaker base or as a wall-mounted option, facial recognition to show your personal messages and calendar, a minimalist touchscreen interface to control locks and thermostats, and FaceTime and intercom calls. The difference has to be in the software and the smart assistant that powers it. Bloomberg reports the smart display will launch with a brand-new homeOS built around Siri AI. Generative AI has breathed new life into the smart home voice assistant by both making it easier to talk to and expanding its capabilities. Until now, Apple’s new Siri AI has been MIA from its HomePods and Apple TV; when you talk to those, the old Siri responds in its basic, functional way. [Image: Apple’s smart speakers: the HomePod and HomePod Mini. Amazon and Google launched theirs last year, but Alexa Plus is only just starting to get it right, and Google’s Gemini for Home, an underpowered version of Gemini, is a confusing mess of capabilities. Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands. So far, every company has hit significant roadblocks bringing a smarter assistant to the home. Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home. These cautious approaches are down to the fact that the home is a big, complicated, messy, multi-user environment that is hard to control. An agentic AI getting something wrong could have consequences far greater than accidentally sending an email. Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems. Every home is different, with unique needs — there is no single plug-and-play solution. Progress has been made toward solving one of the smart home’s biggest challenges: interoperability, with open standards like Matter and Thread promising to make setting up and using a smart home easier. It’s the platforms that have to make the smart home work. Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation. That’s where Siri AI and Apple Intelligence could play a major role. While Apple used Gemini models to build Siri AI, Google itself has struggled to deliver a compelling experience in the home. Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home. This will be the next level for the smart home; with reliable data and context, your home could know who’s in it, where they are, and what they need, and, combined with knowing the status of every device, become proactive. For example, it could alert you that the oven is on and no one is home, suggest turning off the AC when a window is left open, and route messages and notifications to the room you’re in. Today, Apple Home has significant limitations: it doesn’t support every type of home device (no fridges, washing machines, or EV chargers); it can’t control every feature of many device types; and its automations are limited compared to the competition (notably lacking conditional programming options inside the app). All this makes the Home app very easy to use, but extremely underpowered. With Siri AI, Apple could unlock many of those capabilities via voice instead of building complicated menu interfaces.

sources.title: Apple is working with LG on new smart home products, here are the details - GSMArena.com news - GSMArena.com
passages: According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, a very reliable source of Apple-related information, Apple is working with LG on a range of new smart home products.

That said, we're not exactly sure what Apple's involvement will actually be, since these will allegedly be called LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat, and LG Temperature Sensor.
LG has recently sought regulatory approval for these products from the FCC and UL Solutions.
Gurman says LG is handling the manufacturing and product support, even though Apple was (somehow) involved in the development.
Apple has done similar things in the past, working with Belkin and Logitech on accessories.
Such an arrangement gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem "without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories", as Gurman puts it.
Apple can also help "shape the products' design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps".

Apple has done similar things in the past, working with Belkin and Logitech on accessories.
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock diagram (left) and Smart Thermostat diagram (right)

Such an arrangement gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem "without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories", as Gurman puts it. Apple can also help "shape the products' design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps".
A tipster on X has revealed the actual designs of the LG Smart Deadbolt Lock and LG Smart Thermostat. You can see them below.
LG Smart Deadbolt Lock (left) and Smart Thermostat (right)

The lock supports automatic unlocking, tap to unlock, emergency power, and master codes, and it fits 2.375" (60.3mm) and 2.75" (69.9mm) brackets. It comes with two mechanical keys. The Smart Thermostat has settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, and Language, as well as calibrated temperature and temperature offset options.

Mark Gurman says these products won't be released for "at least a few more months", though. Many of these LG-made smart home products will support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Matter, while the door lock should also support UWB for its auto-unlock feature.

Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

Problems with designing its in-house chips have forced Microsoft Corporation to delay its plans and launch an intermediary chip due to competitive fears, suggests a report from The Information. Like Amazon and Google, both of which rely on custom in-house AI processors to reduce reliance on NVIDIA's expensive chips, Microsoft also focuses on in-house chips, but its software-centric business has meant that the firm has few options available. As a result, it aims to catch up with peers and develop alternatives to NVIDIA, but the report suggests that it has had to shake up its plans to accommodate design delays. Today's report builds on an earlier report, also from The Information, which had claimed that Microsoft's Braga AI chip was to delay its mass production from 2025 to 2026. Braga was expected to be a successor to the Microsoft Maia, which was announced in April 2024 and manufactured using TSMC's 5-nanometer manufacturing process. However, according to today's report, Braga's delay led to concerns about the chip's successors, namely Braga-R and Clea, also being delayed. These worries could mean that the chips are not competitive enough with NVIDIA's latest products, and as a result, Microsoft has now purportedly opted for a middle way through which it will launch an AI chip in 2027 that 'lies between' Braga and Braga-R. The Information quotes two sources to share that this new AI chip will likely be called the Maia 280 and link together two Braga chips for greater performance. Like Amazon, Microsoft is also seeking to compete with NVIDIA in performance-per-watt or power efficiency. The firm's executives believe that the new chips can offer as much as 30% improved performance over NVIDIA's 2027 chips. NVIDIA's latest AI chips right now are the Blackwell GPUs, which have started shipping in 2025, and the firm's next-generation AI chips are called Rubin. Microsoft's executives aim to eventually produce hundreds of thousands of in-house AI chips annually. Big tech companies are seeking to diversify away from NVIDIA, with reports suggesting that firms such as Google have started offering their in-house AI chips to computing infrastructure providers for third-party use. The surging interest in custom chips has also led chip designers, such as Broadcom and Marvel, to experience more orders. Marvel's shares closed 2024 88% higher but are down by 33% year-to-date. The stock has suffered as the firm has failed to deliver on lofty investor and analyst AI expectations. While Amazon and Google do rely on in-house AI chips, NVIDIA is nevertheless the indisputable market leader. CEO Jensen Huang believes that custom AI chip projects are struggling due to his company's competitive advantage. While NVIDIA's shares struggled between May and June, they have surged recently to catapult it once again to the top spot in market valuation. Driving the gains are analyst estimates of booming future AI demand and an increased role of GPUs in the global computing infrastructure market. However, the actual improvements users experience will depend on how the chip is deployed and how individual services are optimised.When will Maia 300 be available?Microsoft expects to start deploying Maia 300 in production in 2027, when it also plans to expand its Maia infrastructure to multi-gigawatt scale.- Ends

It could also help the company manage operating expenses, as electricity consumption is a major cost for large data centres.Microsoft introduced its first Maia chip in 2023, followed by Maia 200 in January 2026.

extraction.body: Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

sources.title: Microsoft unveils Maia 300 to cut AI chip dependence on Nvidia and AMD
passages: Microsoft has unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation in-house artificial intelligence chip, as it prepares to rely more on its own hardware to run AI services instead of depending heavily on processors from Nvidia and AMD.

However, the actual improvements users experience will depend on how the chip is deployed and how individual services are optimised.When will Maia 300 be available?Microsoft expects to start deploying Maia 300 in production in 2027, when it also plans to expand its Maia infrastructure to multi-gigawatt scale.- Ends

It could also help the company manage operating expenses, as electricity consumption is a major cost for large data centres.Microsoft introduced its first Maia chip in 2023, followed by Maia 200 in January 2026.

The new chip is designed to handle demanding AI workloads, including complex reasoning, longer conversations and tasks that require AI agents to take multiple steps.The company is using a chiplet-based design for Maia 300, separating computing, memory control and input-output functions.
Microsoft wants its in-house chips to handle a larger share of AI inference, the process through which trained AI models respond to user requests.

extraction.body: Microsoft has unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation in-house artificial intelligence chip, as it prepares to rely more on its own hardware to run AI services instead of depending heavily on processors from Nvidia and AMD. The company plans to begin deploying the new chip in 2027, with the aim of making its Maia family the primary system for handling AI requests across its products and services.Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the launch on X, calling it the company's "biggest bet yet on our own silicon." He said Microsoft would expand its Maia chip deployments to multi-gigawatt capacity starting next year. The move comes as demand for AI computing continues to grow, pushing technology companies to develop their own chips to improve performance and control the cost of running AI services.What makes Maia 300 different from earlier chips?Microsoft says Maia 300 is designed to deliver better performance while using less power. According to the company, the chip is expected to deliver 40 per cent more AI tokens per unit of power than leading GPU-based systems.AI tokens are units of text or data processed by an AI model. Higher token output for the same amount of electricity can help companies run AI services more efficiently.Microsoft also says a data centre rack containing 96 Maia 300 accelerators can deliver up to seven times the token throughput of a comparable Maia 200 configuration. The new chip is designed to handle demanding AI workloads, including complex reasoning, longer conversations and tasks that require AI agents to take multiple steps.The company is using a chiplet-based design for Maia 300, separating computing, memory control and input-output functions. This allows different parts of the chip to use technologies suited to their specific requirements.Will Microsoft stop using Nvidia and AMD chips?Not entirely. Microsoft wants its in-house chips to handle a larger share of AI inference, the process through which trained AI models respond to user requests. However, Nvidia and AMD will continue to play a role in its computing infrastructure, particularly for AI model training.Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) remain widely used for AI workloads, and Microsoft has relied on them to power its cloud services and support AI development.Developing its own processors gives Microsoft another option as demand for computing capacity rises. It could also help the company manage operating expenses, as electricity consumption is a major cost for large data centres.Microsoft introduced its first Maia chip in 2023, followed by Maia 200 in January 2026. The company says Maia 200 is already handling production workloads across services such as Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry.Will Maia 300 make Copilot cheaper or faster?Potentially, but Microsoft has not announced any direct price cuts for customers. Better chip efficiency could reduce the cost of running AI services and allow the company to handle more requests using the same amount of power.Microsoft has also indicated that parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot could become faster with Maia 300. However, the actual improvements users experience will depend on how the chip is deployed and how individual services are optimised.When will Maia 300 be available?Microsoft expects to start deploying Maia 300 in production in 2027, when it also plans to expand its Maia infrastructure to multi-gigawatt scale.- Ends

extraction.body: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan speaks during a joint press conference following the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, established under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, in Istanbul, Turkiye on August 31, 2026. [Arif Hüdaverdi Yaman – Anadolu Agency] The Mecca defense agreement has launched a process to establish a “new security and cooperation architecture” in the region, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Monday, Anadolu reports. Speaking in Istanbul following the first meeting under the trilateral agreement between Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Fidan said: “With this agreement, the process of testing a new security and cooperation architecture in our region has begun.” Regional countries urgently need to act together for security, stability, prosperity and lasting peace, he added. Fidan attended the meeting at Istanbul’s Ciragan Palace alongside Turkish National Defense Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of General Staff Gen. Selcuk Bayraktaroglu. Pakistan’s delegation included Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar, Defense Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. Saudi Arabia was represented by Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan, Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Chief of General Staff Gen. Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili. ‘Alliance established with aim of expanding’ Fidan said the agreement allows other countries to join the alliance, but discussions would be needed with both prospective members and existing members on the conditions, procedures and standards for accession. He said work is underway on a roadmap for the accession process. “The alliance was established with the aim of expanding. But at the outset, its foundations need to be laid very well, and its institutionalization also needs to be carried out very well,” Fidan said, adding that Saudi Arabia and Pakistan also share this sensitivity on the issue. Fidan said the three countries agree on the need to build a strong and institutionalized structure capable of addressing challenges and bringing stability, peace and prosperity to the region, while also expanding the alliance over time. READ: Mecca defense pact has sent ‘message of unity, peace throughout region’: Pakistan premier A potential new ally should join a well-established and effectively functioning structure, he said. “We are now working together to complete the difficult part, which is the establishment phase,” Fidan added. Fidan added that greater stability would create an environment conducive to more investment and development. ‘International system must fight against Netanyahu threat’ Asked about Israel viewing Turkiye as a “strategic threat,” Fidan said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his supporters have increasingly used rhetoric targeting Turkiye, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other Turkish officials as Israel heads into election period. “We have been following this from the beginning,” he said. Fidan described Netanyahu as having become a “common enemy of humanity, the international community and security,” calling him a “criminal” and a “perpetrator of genocide” who should not be taken seriously. He said Netanyahu, his “mentality” and those acting alongside him pose a threat not only to Turkiye but to global security. “It would be a major mistake to think of this as only Turkiye’s problem,” Fidan said. He called on the international community to stop Netanyahu, arguing that his policies are harming the region, Israel, the Jewish people and the wider world. Fidan said Netanyahu’s remarks indicate that he does not want the establishment of a Palestinian state or an end to ongoing occupations in countries across the region. “He wants the genocidal and occupying approach, which endangers regional and international security, to continue,” Fidan said. “This is a major threat not only to us, but to the entire region and the international community. The international system must fight against this threat, this Netanyahu threat,” he added. READ: Report: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to hold first meeting under Joint Defence Agreement

extraction.body: The newly established defense partnership between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is already showing signs of evolving beyond its original three-member format, raising questions over what kind of security architecture could emerge across the Muslim world, and whether Azerbaijan could eventually become part of it. Pakistan has said that six or seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the Mecca Defense Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on August 7. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has similarly indicated that the pact, officially referred to as the Mecca Defense Alliance, is open to expansion. Speaking after the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee under the agreement in Istanbul, Fidan said Türkiye was working on a roadmap for additional members. He also stressed that the alliance "does not nullify or replace our country's obligations arising from NATO, as well as from other alliances and agreements," while arguing that the mechanism could bring "greater stability and reduce uncertainty" to the region. Bangladesh has publicly expressed interest, while Türkiye has also suggested that Egypt could potentially become part of the emerging structure. The alliance's potential expansion raises a particularly important question for Azerbaijan. Baku already maintains close defense ties with all three founding members, while its domestic defense industry has developed rapidly in recent years, particularly in unmanned systems, ammunition, electronic warfare and military modernization. Could that make Azerbaijan more than simply another potential member, and instead a contributor to the alliance's emerging defense-industrial architecture? Asked how likely Azerbaijan is to join the Mecca Defense Alliance, Karauz said: "I consider Azerbaijan to be one of the strongest candidates among potential members. However, in the short term, a close partnership, defense industry cooperation, or a phased integration model before full membership seems more realistic. Azerbaijan’s developing defense relations with both Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia create a favorable environment for this. In particular, Turkish-Azerbaijani defense industry cooperation is already expanding to UAVs, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, communications, and other high-tech areas. Such a model could be formed: Türkiye’s engineering and systems integration + Saudi Arabia’s financial and investment capabilities + Pakistan’s military production and aviation experience + Azerbaijan’s UAVs, ammunition, electronic systems, modernization, and Caucasus-Central Asia connectivity. This could create new markets, joint production opportunities, and technology transfer for Azerbaijan’s rapidly developing domestic defense industry." Yet Karauz cautioned that Baku's decision would not be determined by industrial considerations alone. "However, the key issue in Baku’s decision will not only be the defense industry, but also geopolitical balance. Instead, it will enhance the defense capabilities of regional states, increase their strategic autonomy, and improve their ability to negotiate and maneuver with major powers." However, not all experts are convinced that the Mecca Defense Alliance has reached a stage where its potential expansion or Azerbaijan's participation can be assessed with confidence. Military expert Ramil Mammadli told AzerNEWS that the alliance remains at an early stage and that its members still lack a sufficiently unified strategic agenda: “First of all, I would like to note that since the Mecca Defense Alliance is still a nascent and incomplete format, it is too early to voice optimistic assessments about this alliance. Each of these countries has its own interests in regional issues and needs a common threat in order to act from a single interest. At the moment, there is no such situation, and in this regard, I do not think that Azerbaijani arms manufacturers or the defense industry complex will integrate into the Mecca Defense Alliance as a single structure. Of course, Azerbaijan's defense industry already cooperates with Türkiye and Pakistan, while certain negotiations are underway with Saudi Arabia. If the alliance develops into a genuine unified structure in the future, Azerbaijan, as a defense-industry country, could cooperate with it in specific sectors. Therefore, the future form of this alliance remains uncertain. Mutual defense obligations will become clearer only after we see which other Muslim countries join the process. What form this process will take in the future is among the possibilities. I note once again that mutual defense obligations are only and only related to the participation of other Muslim countries in the process. Of course, we will witness this after a certain period of time." Another interesting element of his assessment concerns the reaction or lack thereof, from major global powers: "The possibilities indicate that so far the US is not an obstacle to this process, which means that it also has certain interests. That is, it will support defense issues and other issues. Also, other major states that are members of NATO do not see any problems in this process. It is interesting that Russia and Iran are not taking any steps to hinder this process. They are simply following these developments in order to obtain information. I believe that this process is aimed at neutralizing Israel at some stage. These are, of course, my personal observations. The opinions expressed by Hakan Fidan at the last meeting of the Foreign Ministers and the harsh statements made towards Israel give reason to say this. Let us take into account that both Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye have very bad relations with Israel and do not accept Israel as a world state at all. In other words, they do not accept it as a normal, civilized world state and have very tense relations. From this point of view, if other Arab countries are to join this alliance, they must participate in the anti-Israel campaign or the anti-Netanyahu campaign. This is one of the main reasons." Mammadli further argued that the emergence of a stronger collective defense mechanism among Muslim-majority countries could challenge existing geopolitical structures: "Of course, fundamentally, the West does not want Islamic countries, especially those with strong foundations and resources located in close proximity, to unite, develop, and be in a single, unified defense format. But it is not in a position to prevent it at this time. Because the West itself is currently in a state of severe confrontation with Russia. I believe that this alliance, this unity in a military format of the Eastern countries, that is, the Islamic, Muslim Eastern countries, is the need of the hour. And the West can take advantage of America's being in a state of severe confrontation with Russia and, taking as a basis the ideas voiced by Israel against Muslim countries, against the Muslim region, against Muslim countries, to represent themselves on a single platform, a military defense platform. In other words, I believe that the West does not intend to take steps to confront this Mecca Defense Alliance on the basis of the current situation. Because if this pressure, such steps are taken, then those countries, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and even Türkiye, may break away from the West, and as a result, those countries may deepen their relations with Russia and China. This may lead to the formation of the next anti-American, anti-Western coalition in the region after Iran." Here we are to serve you with news right now. extraction.body: he Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed on August 7, 2026, in Mecca between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, marks a significant transformation in the security equation between the Middle East and South Asia. At the heart of the agreement lies the principle that an armed attack directed against one of the parties shall be deemed to have been directed against all three states. This provision goes beyond traditional defense cooperation to establish a new security mechanism based on the principle of collective deterrence. The agreement’s primary significance in terms of international relations stems from the convergence of the signatory states’ diverse power elements within a single security framework. Turkey possesses NATO’s second-largest military force, advanced operational capabilities and a defence industry that has grown significantly in recent years. Pakistan is the only Muslim state to possess nuclear weapons. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, stands out for its energy resources, financial capacity and influence in Gulf geopolitics. For this reason, the Mecca Agreement constitutes a strategic configuration of complementary capabilities formed by complementary strategic capabilities, rather than a traditional military alliance between three similar states. The international context in which the agreement emerged is also significant. Rising military tensions in the Middle East, the security of energy transport routes, Iran-centred conflict dynamics and the tendency of regional states to diversify their security guarantees are reinforcing the search for a new regional security order. Within this framework, the Mecca Agreement can be interpreted as a demonstration of the will of regional states to support their security needs increasingly through mechanisms established amongst themselves, rather than through guarantees provided from outside. The concept of strategic autonomy is particularly significant here. Since the end of the Cold War, one of the fundamental pillars of the Middle Eastern security system has been the US military presence and bilateral security relations. The Mecca Agreement does not directly abolish this system. It is also explicitly stated that the parties’ existing bilateral or multilateral obligations remain in force. However, the agreement demonstrates the will of regional actors to establish their own deterrence mechanisms alongside the Washington- centred security architecture. This situation can be interpreted as a transition from a dependence on a single security centre to a multi-layered security architecture. Read: Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan to Sign Joint Defense Pact From Turkey’s perspective, the agreement also has a unique dimension. Turkey is a member of NATO. The Mecca Agreement, whilst enabling Ankara to maintain its NATO membership, also allows it to expand its institutionalised defense relations with regional powers outside NATO. Turkey is thus positioning itself strategically from which it can forge links between the Euro-Atlantic security system and the Middle East–South Asia security spheres. However, the relationship between the collective defense obligation under the Mecca Agreement and Article 5 of the NATO Treaty will require detailed legal and strategic scrutiny in the coming period, particularly in the event of simultaneous crises. Pakistan’s participation in the agreement, meanwhile, shifts the deterrence debate to a different level. Pakistan’s nuclear capability enhances the agreement’s psychological and strategic weight. However, it cannot be concluded from current statements that Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence has been extended to Turkey or Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials have also stated that the agreement is not linked to nuclear purposes or an arms race. Consequently, based on the current data, it does not appear appropriate to characterise the Mecca Agreement as a nuclear umbrella agreement. From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, the agreement represents a continuation of its policy of diversifying security partnerships. By linking its economic capacity with Turkey’s defense industry and Pakistan’s military capabilities, Riyadh may secure a greater degree of strategic manoeuvre. To the extent that this framework extends to areas such as defense industry investments, joint production, technology transfer, training, intelligence sharing and maritime security, it will acquire a lasting institutional character. Read: Why the Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Pact Matters Perhaps the most striking aspect of the Agreement is the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’. This provision is reminiscent of NATO’s logic of collective defense. However, there is currently a significant institutional difference between the two organizations NATO is an institutional alliance with over seventy years’ history, underpinned by a military command structure, joint defense planning, force structure, standards and permanent political bodies. The implementation mechanisms of the Mecca Agreement, however, are not yet as transparent, based on the information made public. For this reason, the true strength of the agreement will be measured not so much by its signing as by the extent to which it becomes institutionalized. Should a joint military committee be established, joint operational plans drawn up, regular exercises conducted, an intelligence-sharing mechanism put in place and defense industry projects undertaken jointly, the Mecca Agreement could evolve into a genuine collective defense system. From Iran’s perspective, interpreting the agreement as a direct counter-alliance requires caution. The parties have specifically emphasized that the agreement does not target any particular state. Given Turkey’s shared border with Iran, its economic ties and regional diplomatic channels, the agreement’s potential to take on a sectarian dimension could entail significant strategic costs for Ankara. Consequently, the sustainability of the agreement will depend on maintaining a balance between the principle of collective defense and the policy of avoiding regional polarization. Read: A New Security Architecture in Afro-Eurasia: The Islamabad Axis of the Tripartite Alliance From Israel’s perspective, the new framework presents a distinct area for strategic calculation. The convergence of Turkey’s NATO capabilities, Pakistan’s military strength and Saudi Arabia’s regional influence within a common security mechanism holds the potential to influence the balance of power in the Middle East. However, it is not possible to draw a definitive conclusion from current statements suggesting that the agreement constitutes an alliance formed against Israel. A broader implication of the Mecca Agreement is the possibility of institutionalizing security cooperation within the Islamic world. Whilst the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is a broad political organization with 57 members, it lacks an effective collective defense mechanism. The tripartite structure emerging in Mecca could, if successful, form the core of a narrower yet highly operational security platform that could expand with the participation of other states. At this point, the fact that the agreement is named ‘Mecca’ also carries symbolic significance. The signing of the agreement at the most important holy centre of the Islamic world lends it political and historical visibility beyond that of a purely military text. However, the agreement’s future legitimacy will be shaped not so much by its symbolic value as by its contribution to regional peace, its compliance with international law, and its capacity to prevent crises. From the perspective of international law, the fundamental basis is the right to individual and collective self-defense, as set out in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Consequently, the pact’s legal legitimacy rests on the organization of collective defense against armed attack, rather than on the formation of an aggressive alliance. In these respects, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement forms a new strategic triangle along the Ankara-Riyadh-Islamabad axis. Turkey’s military and technological capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s economic power and Pakistan’s military-strategic weight are all being integrated into the same security framework. Whether this will evolve into a regional alliance will be determined not so much by the text of the agreement as by the institutions to be established in the future, joint defense plans and the political will demonstrated by the parties in times of crisis. To describe the Mecca Agreement as an ‘Islamic NATO’ at this stage appears premature from an analytical perspective. A more accurate characterization would be that of a new strategic security core, based on regional ownership and collective deterrence, emerging at a time when the US-centered security order is beginning to shift. If the tripartite mechanism becomes institutionalized and expands to include new participants, August 7, 2026, may come to be regarded as one of the starting points of a new era in the Middle East’s security architecture. At the heart of the agreement lies the principle that an armed attack directed against one of the parties shall be deemed to have been directed against all three states. This provision goes beyond traditional defense cooperation to establish a new security mechanism based on the principle of collective deterrence.

The agreement’s primary significance in terms of international relations stems from the convergence of the signatory states’ diverse power elements within a single security framework. Turkey possesses NATO’s second-largest military force, advanced operational capabilities and a defence industry that has grown significantly in recent years. Pakistan is the only Muslim state to possess nuclear weapons. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, stands out for its energy resources, financial capacity and influence in Gulf geopolitics. For this reason, the Mecca Agreement constitutes a strategic configuration of complementary capabilities formed by complementary strategic capabilities, rather than a traditional military alliance between three similar states.

The international context in which the agreement emerged is also significant. Rising military tensions in the Middle East, the security of energy transport routes, Iran-centred conflict dynamics and the tendency of regional states to diversify their security guarantees are reinforcing the search for a new regional security order. Within this framework, the Mecca Agreement can be interpreted as a demonstration of the will of regional states to support their security needs increasingly through mechanisms established amongst themselves, rather than through guarantees provided from outside.

The concept of strategic autonomy is particularly significant here. Since the end of the Cold War, one of the fundamental pillars of the Middle Eastern security system has been the US military presence and bilateral security relations. The Mecca Agreement does not directly abolish this system. It is also explicitly stated that the parties’ existing bilateral or multilateral obligations remain in force. However, the agreement demonstrates the will of regional actors to establish their own deterrence mechanisms alongside the Washington- centred security architecture. This situation can be interpreted as a transition from a dependence on a single security centre to a multi-layered security architecture.

From Turkey’s perspective, the agreement also has a unique dimension. Turkey is a member of NATO. The Mecca Agreement, whilst enabling Ankara to maintain its NATO membership, also allows it to expand its institutionalised defense relations with regional powers outside NATO. Turkey is thus positioning itself strategically from which it can forge links between the Euro-Atlantic security system and the Middle East–South Asia security spheres. However, the relationship between the collective defense obligation under the Mecca Agreement and Article 5 of the NATO Treaty will require detailed legal and strategic scrutiny in the coming period, particularly in the event of simultaneous crises.

Pakistan’s participation in the agreement, meanwhile, shifts the deterrence debate to a different level. Pakistan’s nuclear capability enhances the agreement’s psychological and strategic weight. However, it cannot be concluded from current statements that Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence has been extended to Turkey or Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials have also stated that the agreement is not linked to nuclear purposes or an arms race. Consequently, based on the current data, it does not appear appropriate to characterise the Mecca Agreement as a nuclear umbrella agreement.

From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, the agreement represents a continuation of its policy of diversifying security partnerships. By linking its economic capacity with Turkey’s defense industry and Pakistan’s military capabilities, Riyadh may secure a greater degree of strategic manoeuvre. To the extent that this framework extends to areas such as defense industry investments, joint production, technology transfer, training, intelligence sharing and maritime security, it will acquire a lasting institutional character.
Read: Why the Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Pact Matters

Perhaps the most striking aspect of the Agreement is the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’. This provision is reminiscent of NATO’s logic of collective defense. However, there is currently a significant institutional difference between the two organizations NATO is an institutional alliance with over seventy years’ history, underpinned by a military command structure, joint defense planning, force structure, standards and permanent political bodies. The implementation mechanisms of the Mecca Agreement, however, are not yet as transparent, based on the information made public.

For this reason, the true strength of the agreement will be measured not so much by its signing as by the extent to which it becomes institutionalized. Should a joint military committee be established, joint operational plans drawn up, regular exercises conducted, an intelligence-sharing mechanism put in place and defense industry projects undertaken jointly, the Mecca Agreement could evolve into a genuine collective defense system.

From Iran’s perspective, interpreting the agreement as a direct counter-alliance requires caution. The parties have specifically emphasized that the agreement does not target any particular state. Given Turkey’s shared border with Iran, its economic ties and regional diplomatic channels, the agreement’s potential to take on a sectarian dimension could entail significant strategic costs for Ankara. Consequently, the sustainability of the agreement will depend on maintaining a balance between the principle of collective defense and the policy of avoiding regional polarization.

From Israel’s perspective, the new framework presents a distinct area for strategic calculation. The convergence of Turkey’s NATO capabilities, Pakistan’s military strength and Saudi Arabia’s regional influence within a common security mechanism holds the potential to influence the balance of power in the Middle East. However, it is not possible to draw a definitive conclusion from current statements suggesting that the agreement constitutes an alliance formed against Israel.

A broader implication of the Mecca Agreement is the possibility of institutionalizing security cooperation within the Islamic world. Whilst the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is a broad political organization with 57 members, it lacks an effective collective defense mechanism. The tripartite structure emerging in Mecca could, if successful, form the core of a narrower yet highly operational security platform that could expand with the participation of other states.

At this point, the fact that the agreement is named ‘Mecca’ also carries symbolic significance. The signing of the agreement at the most important holy centre of the Islamic world lends it political and historical visibility beyond that of a purely military text. However, the agreement’s future legitimacy will be shaped not so much by its symbolic value as by its contribution to regional peace, its compliance with international law, and its capacity to prevent crises.

From the perspective of international law, the fundamental basis is the right to individual and collective self-defense, as set out in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Consequently, the pact’s legal legitimacy rests on the organization of collective defense against armed attack, rather than on the formation of an aggressive alliance.

In these respects, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement forms a new strategic triangle along the Ankara-Riyadh-Islamabad axis. Turkey’s military and technological capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s economic power and Pakistan’s military-strategic weight are all being integrated into the same security framework. Whether this will evolve into a regional alliance will be determined not so much by the text of the agreement as by the institutions to be established in the future, joint defense plans and the political will demonstrated by the parties in times of crisis.

A more accurate characterization would be that of a new strategic security core, based on regional ownership and collective deterrence, emerging at a time when the US-centered security order is beginning to shift. If the tripartite mechanism becomes institutionalized and expands to include new participants, August 7, 2026, may come to be regarded as one of the starting points of a new era in the Middle East’s security architecture.

extraction.body: After more than a year of talks , Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact last week in Mecca. Bringing together Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim country, Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters and custodian of Islam’s holiest sites, and Turkey, NATO’s second-largest military, the agreement marks a significant shift in the regional security architecture . The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all, echoing NATO’s Article 5. It also builds on the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) signed by Riyadh and Islamabad last September. Unlike that bilateral accord, however, the new arrangement could be expanded to include other countries. Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, stressed that the agreement does not “supersede or replace” existing bilateral or multilateral arrangements. Nor, he said, is it linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race, but rather to building “sustainable capabilities”. He was equally pointed that the pact was not an escalation between any two states or a threat to any country in the region. This careful language suggests that the pact is intended less as a military coalition against Iran, Israel or any other specific adversary, than an attempt to build a more durable regional security order based on mutual defence and non-aggression. That ambition has gained urgency. The Iran conflict has exposed the fragility of the region’s existing security arrangements, while uncertainty over the reliability of external security guarantees has grown. Houthi threats to Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping routes have added another layer of vulnerability. Torek Farhadi, a senior geo-economic advisor based in Geneva, told The New Arab that the “sheer fact that these three countries are aligned in their political thinking is by itself a stabilising factor in an otherwise fractured Middle East”. With Turkey and Pakistan both energy-importing countries, Saudi Arabia provides their economies with important resource security. Turkey being a NATO member, meanwhile, is positively viewed by Western capitals as a “provider of much-needed stability”, Farhadi said. But it was the maturation of “two bilateral tracks that laid the political and military groundwork necessary for the Joint Defence Agreement signed in Mecca,” Zeynep Gizem Ozpinar, a Turkish foreign policy expert , told The New Arab . In her opinion, the complementary capacities of the three countries are “Turkey’s defence industry and operational experience, Saudi Arabia’s financial strength and strategic geography, and Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence”. The Mecca pact has brought together relationships that had previously advanced along separate channels within a shared strategic framework. Explaining the depth of ties, Ozpinar noted that Turkey’s defence relationship with Pakistan rests on a foundation spanning decades, nourished by a discourse of brotherhood and gradually institutionalised over time. Ankara’s ties with Riyadh, meanwhile, have undergone a visible process of “normalisation and rapprochement” in recent years. Reciprocal high-level visits, memoranda signed in the defence sector, and a rising volume of trade have all served as concrete indicators of trust-building on the Ankara-Riyadh axis, she said. Where Saudi-Turkish ties are concerned, Ozpinar said that it was “Riyadh’s pursuit of strategic depth in the face of uncertainties within the regional security environment” that produced “favourable ground that aligns with Turkey’s defence industry capacity”. Looking ahead, Junaid Javeed, a risk and security management expert, told The New Arab that the Mecca agreement has the potential to alter the strategic equation across a region stretching from the eastern Mediterranean to the northern Indian Ocean. After the storm: The Gulf states in a post-Iran war region Comparing the Mecca pact with NATO, Javeed said that the latter has more than just a mutual defence clause. “It is a deeply institutionalised alliance with established command structures, planning mechanisms and decades of operational integration, and the Mecca alliance is not on that level yet,” he told The New Arab . Assessing the geopolitical impact of this agreement, Javeed said that Iran would “closely watch the agreement’s Gulf and maritime potential” while India would “assess what it means for Pakistan’s strategic capabilities”. China, he said, will have “an interest in its effect on Gulf stability, while the United States will consider whether the arrangement strengthens or complicates the existing regional security architecture”, Javeed added. While a political commitment has been created, the real challenge is building the machinery to get “military credibility”. Nevertheless, with Pakistan’s position on the Arabian Sea, Saudi Arabia’s strategic access to the Gulf and Red Sea, and Turkey’s naval capabilities, the three countries naturally complement each other. Seeking regional stability rather than getting into unwanted war scenarios, this trilateral accord may remain focused on proactive defence. But if implemented effectively, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan agreement could rebalance the Middle East. Ostensibly, Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, diplomatic influence, and its central role in Gulf security. Turkey offers one of NATO's most capable militaries alongside a rapidly expanding indigenous defence industry that has emerged as a global exporter of drones, missiles, naval platforms, and armoured vehicles. Meanwhile, Pakistan provides one of the region's largest and most experienced armed forces, extensive counterterrorism expertise, and the unique status of being the only nuclear-armed Muslim state. Discussing the implications of the deal for Pakistan, Abdullah Khan , Managing Director at the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies in Islamabad, told The New Arab that the trilateral defence MoU significantly strengthens Pakistan’s strategic standing both in the Gulf and across South Asia. “The space Pakistan had progressively lost to India in the Middle East is being reclaimed - and in many ways exceeded - through this institutionalised partnership with two major regional powers,” Khan told The New Arab . The agreement will also have an impact in South Asia, creating “new openings for Pakistan-India dialogue as Saudi Arabia, bound by mutual defence commitments with Pakistan, has no interest in being drawn into a military confrontation involving India”. The Middle East's race to bypass the Strait of Hormuz More countries will likely join the Mecca alliance, and it is expected to be a more flexible security partnership than a focused military alliance, as the ethos of the grouping is going to remain “collective deterrence”. In line with Turkey’s defence diplomacy and Pakistan’s customised security deals with regional states, it may turn out to be a win-win situation. Putting less pressure on the US, which would continue as a main security guarantor, and, hopefully, keeping oil routes open for the GCC, the Mecca alliance may be exactly what the region needs. The pact could extend beyond these three initial signatories and a wider trend could emerge whereby local states would “seek greater control over their own defence”, Javeed told The New Arab . “Operating within a framework built on the principle of collective deterrence, Turkey is opening new markets for its defence industry exports and positioning itself as one of the founding actors in the emerging security architecture of the Islamic world.” She noted that this could be regarded as a “natural extension of the multidimensional, multi-vector foreign policy approach Ankara has pursued for some time, and the defence industry dimension constitutes the most tangible aspect of these gains”. Pakistan’s large military and missile technology further completes this picture.

At this point, the fact that the agreement is named ‘Mecca’ also carries symbolic significance.

“It is a deeply institutionalised alliance with established command structures, planning mechanisms and decades of operational integration, and the Mecca alliance is not on that level yet,” he told The New Arab .
Seeking regional stability rather than getting into unwanted war scenarios, this trilateral accord may remain focused on proactive defence.
But if implemented effectively, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan agreement could rebalance the Middle East.
After more than a year of talks , Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact last week in Mecca.

Where Saudi-Turkish ties are concerned, Ozpinar said that it was “Riyadh’s pursuit of strategic depth in the face of uncertainties within the regional security environment” that produced “favourable ground that aligns with Turkey’s defence industry capacity”.

China, he said, will have “an interest in its effect on Gulf stability, while the United States will consider whether the arrangement strengthens or complicates the existing regional security architecture”, Javeed added.

“Operating within a framework built on the principle of collective deterrence, Turkey is opening new markets for its defence industry exports and positioning itself as one of the founding actors in the emerging security architecture of the Islamic world.”

Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili. ‘Alliance established with aim of expanding’ Fidan said the agreement allows other countries to join the alliance, but discussions would be needed with both prospective members and existing members on the conditions, procedures and standards for accession. But at the outset, its foundations need to be laid very well, and its institutionalization also needs to be carried out very well,” Fidan said, adding that Saudi Arabia and Pakistan also share this sensitivity on the issue. Fidan said Netanyahu’s remarks indicate that he does not want the establishment of a Palestinian state or an end to ongoing occupations in countries across the region. “He wants the genocidal and occupying approach, which endangers regional and international security, to continue,” Fidan said. “This is a major threat not only to us, but to the entire region and the international community. extraction.body: The newly established defense partnership between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan is already showing signs of evolving beyond its original three-member format, raising questions over what kind of security architecture could emerge across the Muslim world, and whether Azerbaijan could eventually become part of it. Pakistan has said that six or seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the Mecca Defense Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on August 7. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has similarly indicated that the pact, officially referred to as the Mecca Defense Alliance, is open to expansion. Speaking after the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee under the agreement in Istanbul, Fidan said Türkiye was working on a roadmap for additional members. He also stressed that the alliance "does not nullify or replace our country's obligations arising from NATO, as well as from other alliances and agreements," while arguing that the mechanism could bring "greater stability and reduce uncertainty" to the region. Bangladesh has publicly expressed interest, while Türkiye has also suggested that Egypt could potentially become part of the emerging structure. The alliance's potential expansion raises a particularly important question for Azerbaijan. Baku already maintains close defense ties with all three founding members, while its domestic defense industry has developed rapidly in recent years, particularly in unmanned systems, ammunition, electronic warfare and military modernization. Could that make Azerbaijan more than simply another potential member, and instead a contributor to the alliance's emerging defense-industrial architecture? Speaking to AzerNEWS , former military attaché and retired General Yücel Karauz believes Azerbaijan is among the strongest candidates for closer integration, although he sees full membership as a longer-term possibility. Asked how likely Azerbaijan is to join the Mecca Defense Alliance, Karauz said: "I consider Azerbaijan to be one of the strongest candidates among potential members. However, in the short term, a close partnership, defense industry cooperation, or a phased integration model before full membership seems more realistic. Azerbaijan’s developing defense relations with both Türkiye, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia create a favorable environment for this. In particular, Turkish-Azerbaijani defense industry cooperation is already expanding to UAVs, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, communications, and other high-tech areas. If Azerbaijan joins this alliance, its role should not be limited to being only an arms buyer. Baku could become one of the production and technology centers of the new defense industry supply chain. Such a model could be formed: Türkiye’s engineering and systems integration + Saudi Arabia’s financial and investment capabilities + Pakistan’s military production and aviation experience + Azerbaijan’s UAVs, ammunition, electronic systems, modernization, and Caucasus-Central Asia connectivity. This could create new markets, joint production opportunities, and technology transfer for Azerbaijan’s rapidly developing domestic defense industry." Yet Karauz cautioned that Baku's decision would not be determined by industrial considerations alone. "However, the key issue in Baku’s decision will not only be the defense industry, but also geopolitical balance. Azerbaijan, while maintaining its strategic alliance with Türkiye, must also take into account its room for maneuver in its relations with Russia, Iran, Israel, and the countries of Central Asia. Therefore, in my assessment, the likelihood of Azerbaijan’s integration into the defense industry and military cooperation mechanisms of the alliance is high, and full collective defense membership in the short term is moderate." Can the alliance expand without losing cohesion? Karauz argues that the answer is not necessarily to impose identical responsibilities on every member. "One of the greatest challenges for the Mecca Alliance will be expansion. The accession of Bangladesh, Egypt and other Muslim countries will increase the political and strategic weight of the alliance. However, as the number of members increases, differences in military standards, threat perceptions and national interests will also increase. Therefore, the most correct model is not to give all members the same military function, but to create a phased military integration within the framework of a single collective defense. The Türkiye-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan triad should remain the main core of the alliance. This triad can play a leading role in: command and control, intelligence exchange, air and missile defense, joint military exercises, logistics and the formation of defense industry standards. New members should be gradually included in the system based on their levels of military readiness and technical compatibility. The most important issue is to determine in advance and precisely under what conditions the collective defense mechanism will be activated. The permanent secretariat planned for Riyadh could play a major role in determining whether the alliance remains primarily political or develops into a functional military structure." Karauz also believes its institutional role should extend beyond diplomacy. "The permanent secretariat to be established in Riyadh is of great importance in this regard.
