extraction.body: he Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed on August 7, 2026, in Mecca between Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, marks a significant transformation in the security equation between the Middle East and South Asia. At the heart of the agreement lies the principle that an armed attack directed against one of the parties shall be deemed to have been directed against all three states. This provision goes beyond traditional defense cooperation to establish a new security mechanism based on the principle of collective deterrence. The agreement’s primary significance in terms of international relations stems from the convergence of the signatory states’ diverse power elements within a single security framework. Turkey possesses NATO’s second-largest military force, advanced operational capabilities and a defence industry that has grown significantly in recent years. Pakistan is the only Muslim state to possess nuclear weapons. Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, stands out for its energy resources, financial capacity and influence in Gulf geopolitics. For this reason, the Mecca Agreement constitutes a strategic configuration of complementary capabilities formed by complementary strategic capabilities, rather than a traditional military alliance between three similar states. The international context in which the agreement emerged is also significant. Rising military tensions in the Middle East, the security of energy transport routes, Iran-centred conflict dynamics and the tendency of regional states to diversify their security guarantees are reinforcing the search for a new regional security order. Within this framework, the Mecca Agreement can be interpreted as a demonstration of the will of regional states to support their security needs increasingly through mechanisms established amongst themselves, rather than through guarantees provided from outside. The concept of strategic autonomy is particularly significant here. Since the end of the Cold War, one of the fundamental pillars of the Middle Eastern security system has been the US military presence and bilateral security relations. The Mecca Agreement does not directly abolish this system. It is also explicitly stated that the parties’ existing bilateral or multilateral obligations remain in force. However, the agreement demonstrates the will of regional actors to establish their own deterrence mechanisms alongside the Washington- centred security architecture. This situation can be interpreted as a transition from a dependence on a single security centre to a multi-layered security architecture. Read: Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan to Sign Joint Defense Pact From Turkey’s perspective, the agreement also has a unique dimension. Turkey is a member of NATO. The Mecca Agreement, whilst enabling Ankara to maintain its NATO membership, also allows it to expand its institutionalised defense relations with regional powers outside NATO. Turkey is thus positioning itself strategically from which it can forge links between the Euro-Atlantic security system and the Middle East–South Asia security spheres. However, the relationship between the collective defense obligation under the Mecca Agreement and Article 5 of the NATO Treaty will require detailed legal and strategic scrutiny in the coming period, particularly in the event of simultaneous crises. Pakistan’s participation in the agreement, meanwhile, shifts the deterrence debate to a different level. Pakistan’s nuclear capability enhances the agreement’s psychological and strategic weight. However, it cannot be concluded from current statements that Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence has been extended to Turkey or Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials have also stated that the agreement is not linked to nuclear purposes or an arms race. Consequently, based on the current data, it does not appear appropriate to characterise the Mecca Agreement as a nuclear umbrella agreement. From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, the agreement represents a continuation of its policy of diversifying security partnerships. By linking its economic capacity with Turkey’s defense industry and Pakistan’s military capabilities, Riyadh may secure a greater degree of strategic manoeuvre. To the extent that this framework extends to areas such as defense industry investments, joint production, technology transfer, training, intelligence sharing and maritime security, it will acquire a lasting institutional character. Read: Why the Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Pact Matters Perhaps the most striking aspect of the Agreement is the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’. This provision is reminiscent of NATO’s logic of collective defense. However, there is currently a significant institutional difference between the two organizations NATO is an institutional alliance with over seventy years’ history, underpinned by a military command structure, joint defense planning, force structure, standards and permanent political bodies. The implementation mechanisms of the Mecca Agreement, however, are not yet as transparent, based on the information made public. For this reason, the true strength of the agreement will be measured not so much by its signing as by the extent to which it becomes institutionalized. Should a joint military committee be established, joint operational plans drawn up, regular exercises conducted, an intelligence-sharing mechanism put in place and defense industry projects undertaken jointly, the Mecca Agreement could evolve into a genuine collective defense system. From Iran’s perspective, interpreting the agreement as a direct counter-alliance requires caution. The parties have specifically emphasized that the agreement does not target any particular state. Given Turkey’s shared border with Iran, its economic ties and regional diplomatic channels, the agreement’s potential to take on a sectarian dimension could entail significant strategic costs for Ankara. Consequently, the sustainability of the agreement will depend on maintaining a balance between the principle of collective defense and the policy of avoiding regional polarization. Read: A New Security Architecture in Afro-Eurasia: The Islamabad Axis of the Tripartite Alliance From Israel’s perspective, the new framework presents a distinct area for strategic calculation. The convergence of Turkey’s NATO capabilities, Pakistan’s military strength and Saudi Arabia’s regional influence within a common security mechanism holds the potential to influence the balance of power in the Middle East. However, it is not possible to draw a definitive conclusion from current statements suggesting that the agreement constitutes an alliance formed against Israel. A broader implication of the Mecca Agreement is the possibility of institutionalizing security cooperation within the Islamic world. Whilst the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is a broad political organization with 57 members, it lacks an effective collective defense mechanism. The tripartite structure emerging in Mecca could, if successful, form the core of a narrower yet highly operational security platform that could expand with the participation of other states. At this point, the fact that the agreement is named ‘Mecca’ also carries symbolic significance. The signing of the agreement at the most important holy centre of the Islamic world lends it political and historical visibility beyond that of a purely military text. However, the agreement’s future legitimacy will be shaped not so much by its symbolic value as by its contribution to regional peace, its compliance with international law, and its capacity to prevent crises. From the perspective of international law, the fundamental basis is the right to individual and collective self-defense, as set out in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Consequently, the pact’s legal legitimacy rests on the organization of collective defense against armed attack, rather than on the formation of an aggressive alliance. In these respects, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement forms a new strategic triangle along the Ankara-Riyadh-Islamabad axis. Turkey’s military and technological capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s economic power and Pakistan’s military-strategic weight are all being integrated into the same security framework. Whether this will evolve into a regional alliance will be determined not so much by the text of the agreement as by the institutions to be established in the future, joint defense plans and the political will demonstrated by the parties in times of crisis. To describe the Mecca Agreement as an ‘Islamic NATO’ at this stage appears premature from an analytical perspective. A more accurate characterization would be that of a new strategic security core, based on regional ownership and collective deterrence, emerging at a time when the US-centered security order is beginning to shift. If the tripartite mechanism becomes institutionalized and expands to include new participants, August 7, 2026, may come to be regarded as one of the starting points of a new era in the Middle East’s security architecture. However, the agreement demonstrates the will of regional actors to establish their own deterrence mechanisms alongside the Washington- centred security architecture. This situation can be interpreted as a transition from a dependence on a single security centre to a multi-layered security architecture.
Read: Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan to Sign Joint Defense Pact

From Turkey’s perspective, the agreement also has a unique dimension. Turkey is a member of NATO. The Mecca Agreement, whilst enabling Ankara to maintain its NATO membership, also allows it to expand its institutionalised defense relations with regional powers outside NATO. Turkey is thus positioning itself strategically from which it can forge links between the Euro-Atlantic security system and the Middle East–South Asia security spheres. However, the relationship between the collective defense obligation under the Mecca Agreement and Article 5 of the NATO Treaty will require detailed legal and strategic scrutiny in the coming period, particularly in the event of simultaneous crises.

Pakistan’s participation in the agreement, meanwhile, shifts the deterrence debate to a different level. Pakistan’s nuclear capability enhances the agreement’s psychological and strategic weight. However, it cannot be concluded from current statements that Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence has been extended to Turkey or Saudi Arabia. Saudi officials have also stated that the agreement is not linked to nuclear purposes or an arms race. Consequently, based on the current data, it does not appear appropriate to characterise the Mecca Agreement as a nuclear umbrella agreement.

From Saudi Arabia’s perspective, the agreement represents a continuation of its policy of diversifying security partnerships. By linking its economic capacity with Turkey’s defense industry and Pakistan’s military capabilities, Riyadh may secure a greater degree of strategic manoeuvre. To the extent that this framework extends to areas such as defense industry investments, joint production, technology transfer, training, intelligence sharing and maritime security, it will acquire a lasting institutional character.
Read: Why the Türkiye-Saudi-Pakistan Pact Matters

Perhaps the most striking aspect of the Agreement is the principle of ‘an attack on one is an attack on all’. This provision is reminiscent of NATO’s logic of collective defense. However, there is currently a significant institutional difference between the two organizations NATO is an institutional alliance with over seventy years’ history, underpinned by a military command structure, joint defense planning, force structure, standards and permanent political bodies. The implementation mechanisms of the Mecca Agreement, however, are not yet as transparent, based on the information made public.

For this reason, the true strength of the agreement will be measured not so much by its signing as by the extent to which it becomes institutionalized. Should a joint military committee be established, joint operational plans drawn up, regular exercises conducted, an intelligence-sharing mechanism put in place and defense industry projects undertaken jointly, the Mecca Agreement could evolve into a genuine collective defense system.

From Iran’s perspective, interpreting the agreement as a direct counter-alliance requires caution. The parties have specifically emphasized that the agreement does not target any particular state. Given Turkey’s shared border with Iran, its economic ties and regional diplomatic channels, the agreement’s potential to take on a sectarian dimension could entail significant strategic costs for Ankara. Consequently, the sustainability of the agreement will depend on maintaining a balance between the principle of collective defense and the policy of avoiding regional polarization.
Read: A New Security Architecture in Afro-Eurasia: The Islamabad Axis of the Tripartite Alliance

From Israel’s perspective, the new framework presents a distinct area for strategic calculation. The convergence of Turkey’s NATO capabilities, Pakistan’s military strength and Saudi Arabia’s regional influence within a common security mechanism holds the potential to influence the balance of power in the Middle East. However, it is not possible to draw a definitive conclusion from current statements suggesting that the agreement constitutes an alliance formed against Israel.

A broader implication of the Mecca Agreement is the possibility of institutionalizing security cooperation within the Islamic world. Whilst the Organization of Islamic Cooperation is a broad political organization with 57 members, it lacks an effective collective defense mechanism. The tripartite structure emerging in Mecca could, if successful, form the core of a narrower yet highly operational security platform that could expand with the participation of other states.

At this point, the fact that the agreement is named ‘Mecca’ also carries symbolic significance. The signing of the agreement at the most important holy centre of the Islamic world lends it political and historical visibility beyond that of a purely military text. However, the agreement’s future legitimacy will be shaped not so much by its symbolic value as by its contribution to regional peace, its compliance with international law, and its capacity to prevent crises.

From the perspective of international law, the fundamental basis is the right to individual and collective self-defense, as set out in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. Consequently, the pact’s legal legitimacy rests on the organization of collective defense against armed attack, rather than on the formation of an aggressive alliance.

In these respects, the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement forms a new strategic triangle along the Ankara-Riyadh-Islamabad axis. Turkey’s military and technological capabilities, Saudi Arabia’s economic power and Pakistan’s military-strategic weight are all being integrated into the same security framework. Whether this will evolve into a regional alliance will be determined not so much by the text of the agreement as by the institutions to be established in the future, joint defense plans and the political will demonstrated by the parties in times of crisis.

To describe the Mecca Agreement as an ‘Islamic NATO’ at this stage appears premature from an analytical perspective. A more accurate characterization would be that of a new strategic security core, based on regional ownership and collective deterrence, emerging at a time when the US-centered security order is beginning to shift. If the tripartite mechanism becomes institutionalized and expands to include new participants, August 7, 2026, may come to be regarded as one of the starting points of a new era in the Middle East’s security architecture.

He worked as a Denizcilik Uzman (Maritime Expert) at the Denizcilik Müsteşarlığı (Ministry of Maritime Affairs), as a Daire Başkanı (Director) at the Ulaştırma ve Altyapı Bakanlığı (Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure) and as an I. Hukuk Müşaviri (Senior Legal Advisor) at the Enerji ve Tabii Kaynaklar Bakanlığı (Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources). During this period, he was appointed as a member of the Atomic Energy Commission at the Turkey Atomic Energy Agency. After serving as a member of the Energy Market Regulation Board (EPDK) in 2018, he was appointed as the General Director of the Treasury and Finance Ministry's Chief Legal Advisor and Litigation Department. He continues to work as the Chairman of the Audit Committee and the Chairman of the Legal Working Group at the World Energy Council Turkish National Committee (WEC-TMK). He was elected to the TCMB Denetleme Kurulu in 2019 and was reelected to the same position in the TCMB Olağan Genel Kurulu in 2021. Additionally, Kurt served as the President of the Mali Suçları Araştırma Kurulu (MASAK) of the T.C. Ministry of Finance from 2020 to 2022 and as the President of the Kamu Gözetimi Muhasebe ve Denetim Standartları Kurumu from 2022.

extraction.body: After more than a year of talks , Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a landmark defence pact last week in Mecca. Bringing together Pakistan, the only nuclear-armed Muslim country, Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters and custodian of Islam’s holiest sites, and Turkey, NATO’s second-largest military, the agreement marks a significant shift in the regional security architecture . The pact stipulates that an armed attack against one of the three countries would be treated as an attack against all, echoing NATO’s Article 5. It also builds on the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) signed by Riyadh and Islamabad last September. Unlike that bilateral accord, however, the new arrangement could be expanded to include other countries. Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, stressed that the agreement does not “supersede or replace” existing bilateral or multilateral arrangements. Nor, he said, is it linked to nuclear ambitions or an arms race, but rather to building “sustainable capabilities”. He was equally pointed that the pact was not an escalation between any two states or a threat to any country in the region. This careful language suggests that the pact is intended less as a military coalition against Iran, Israel or any other specific adversary, than an attempt to build a more durable regional security order based on mutual defence and non-aggression. That ambition has gained urgency. The Iran conflict has exposed the fragility of the region’s existing security arrangements, while uncertainty over the reliability of external security guarantees has grown. Houthi threats to Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping routes have added another layer of vulnerability. Torek Farhadi, a senior geo-economic advisor based in Geneva, told The New Arab that the “sheer fact that these three countries are aligned in their political thinking is by itself a stabilising factor in an otherwise fractured Middle East”. With Turkey and Pakistan both energy-importing countries, Saudi Arabia provides their economies with important resource security. Turkey being a NATO member, meanwhile, is positively viewed by Western capitals as a “provider of much-needed stability”, Farhadi said. But it was the maturation of “two bilateral tracks that laid the political and military groundwork necessary for the Joint Defence Agreement signed in Mecca,” Zeynep Gizem Ozpinar, a Turkish foreign policy expert , told The New Arab . In her opinion, the complementary capacities of the three countries are “Turkey’s defence industry and operational experience, Saudi Arabia’s financial strength and strategic geography, and Pakistan’s nuclear deterrence”. The Mecca pact has brought together relationships that had previously advanced along separate channels within a shared strategic framework. Explaining the depth of ties, Ozpinar noted that Turkey’s defence relationship with Pakistan rests on a foundation spanning decades, nourished by a discourse of brotherhood and gradually institutionalised over time. Ankara’s ties with Riyadh, meanwhile, have undergone a visible process of “normalisation and rapprochement” in recent years. Reciprocal high-level visits, memoranda signed in the defence sector, and a rising volume of trade have all served as concrete indicators of trust-building on the Ankara-Riyadh axis, she said. Where Saudi-Turkish ties are concerned, Ozpinar said that it was “Riyadh’s pursuit of strategic depth in the face of uncertainties within the regional security environment” that produced “favourable ground that aligns with Turkey’s defence industry capacity”. Looking ahead, Junaid Javeed, a risk and security management expert, told The New Arab that the Mecca agreement has the potential to alter the strategic equation across a region stretching from the eastern Mediterranean to the northern Indian Ocean. After the storm: The Gulf states in a post-Iran war region Comparing the Mecca pact with NATO, Javeed said that the latter has more than just a mutual defence clause. “It is a deeply institutionalised alliance with established command structures, planning mechanisms and decades of operational integration, and the Mecca alliance is not on that level yet,” he told The New Arab . Assessing the geopolitical impact of this agreement, Javeed said that Iran would “closely watch the agreement’s Gulf and maritime potential” while India would “assess what it means for Pakistan’s strategic capabilities”. China, he said, will have “an interest in its effect on Gulf stability, while the United States will consider whether the arrangement strengthens or complicates the existing regional security architecture”, Javeed added. While a political commitment has been created, the real challenge is building the machinery to get “military credibility”. Nevertheless, with Pakistan’s position on the Arabian Sea, Saudi Arabia’s strategic access to the Gulf and Red Sea, and Turkey’s naval capabilities, the three countries naturally complement each other. Seeking regional stability rather than getting into unwanted war scenarios, this trilateral accord may remain focused on proactive defence. But if implemented effectively, the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan agreement could rebalance the Middle East. Ostensibly, Saudi Arabia contributes financial resources, diplomatic influence, and its central role in Gulf security. Turkey offers one of NATO's most capable militaries alongside a rapidly expanding indigenous defence industry that has emerged as a global exporter of drones, missiles, naval platforms, and armoured vehicles. Meanwhile, Pakistan provides one of the region's largest and most experienced armed forces, extensive counterterrorism expertise, and the unique status of being the only nuclear-armed Muslim state. Discussing the implications of the deal for Pakistan, Abdullah Khan , Managing Director at the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies in Islamabad, told The New Arab that the trilateral defence MoU significantly strengthens Pakistan’s strategic standing both in the Gulf and across South Asia. “The space Pakistan had progressively lost to India in the Middle East is being reclaimed - and in many ways exceeded - through this institutionalised partnership with two major regional powers,” Khan told The New Arab . The agreement will also have an impact in South Asia, creating “new openings for Pakistan-India dialogue as Saudi Arabia, bound by mutual defence commitments with Pakistan, has no interest in being drawn into a military confrontation involving India”. The Middle East's race to bypass the Strait of Hormuz More countries will likely join the Mecca alliance, and it is expected to be a more flexible security partnership than a focused military alliance, as the ethos of the grouping is going to remain “collective deterrence”. In line with Turkey’s defence diplomacy and Pakistan’s customised security deals with regional states, it may turn out to be a win-win situation. Putting less pressure on the US, which would continue as a main security guarantor, and, hopefully, keeping oil routes open for the GCC, the Mecca alliance may be exactly what the region needs. The pact could extend beyond these three initial signatories and a wider trend could emerge whereby local states would “seek greater control over their own defence”, Javeed told The New Arab . “Operating within a framework built on the principle of collective deterrence, Turkey is opening new markets for its defence industry exports and positioning itself as one of the founding actors in the emerging security architecture of the Islamic world.” She noted that this could be regarded as a “natural extension of the multidimensional, multi-vector foreign policy approach Ankara has pursued for some time, and the defence industry dimension constitutes the most tangible aspect of these gains”. Pakistan’s large military and missile technology further completes this picture.

(NASDAQ: FFAI) (“Faraday Future,” “FF,” or the “Company”), a California -based global Embodied AI (“EAI”) ecosystem company, today announced that this week’s Investor Weekly Report from FF Founder and Global CEO YT Jia has been rescheduled to October 14.
Faraday Future Announces This Week’s Investor Weekly Report from YT Jia Has Been Rescheduled to October 14; FFR and FFAI to Host Joint New Product Launch Event on October 14

Additionally, FFR and FFAI will host a joint new product launch event on October 14, 2026, featuring four major launches focused on embodied AI robotics, Physical AI education, and developer enablement.
The event will feature FF Nova, FF’s first embodied AI humanoid robot designed for developers and educational institutions, through an exclusive, invitation-only launch.
FF will also introduce FF Nova Mini, a humanoid robot designed for foundational Physical AI education, as well as the EAI Education Ecosystem Brain and Curriculum Skills 2.0.
In addition, FF will launch the FF Nova Developer Reinforcement Learning Platform and open exclusive early access to the developer community.
Investors (English): ir@ff.com Investors (Chinese): cn-ir@faradayfuture.com Media: john.schilling@ff.com
Source: Faraday Future Intelligent Electric Inc.

passages: Apple has set 13 October for a ‘Welcome home’ launch, and the rumours all point to smart home hardware.
In a post on X, Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, teased the company’s next reveal with a short video and four words: “Welcome home.
Invitations have also gone to some members of the press for an “Apple Experience” in Tribeca, New York, starting at 9:00 a.m.
ET on 13 October, as shared by Marques Brownlee .
9to5Mac notes that Apple ran a similar hands-on session for the MacBook Neo earlier this year.
Welcome home. October 13. pic.twitter.com/ChelGSDOTI
9to5Mac also expects the LG-made smart lock and thermostat that leaked recently to appear, since Apple reportedly co-developed them with LG.
MacRumors says the hub has been ready for months and was waiting on Siri AI, which TechRadar notes arrived last month with iOS 27.
The launch also follows our look at the three Apple launches to watch this month .
Apple hasn’t said where the products will go on sale, or at what price.
Pricing so far is a US rumour only, so there is no UAE figure to cite yet.
Everything below comes from rumours and code leaks, not Apple.

sources.title: Apple 10월 13일 이벤트 공식 확정: Welcome Home과 주목할 신제품 7종
passages: 빠른 답변 Apple이 2026년 10월 13일 ‘Welcome home’ 신제품 공개를 공식 확인했습니다. 초대장에 따르면 뉴욕 트라이베카에서 Apple Experience가 열리며 시작 시간은 미국 동부시간 오전 9시. 주목할 제품은 신형 Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, 그리고 HomePad로 불리는 스마트 홈 디스플레이입니다. 이후 10월 말에는 Mac과 iPad 4개 제품군이 추가 공개될 것으로 보도됐지만, 해당 라인업은 Apple이 확인하지 않았습니다. 구매를 미룰 수 있다면 Apple TV나 HomePod mini를 사기 전에 10월 13일 발표를 확인하세요.

October 13.” MacRumors: 10월 13일 제품 공개 공식 발표 MacRumors: 10월 13일 스마트 홈 프리뷰 MacRumors: 10월 말 MacBook Pro·iPad mini 공개 보도 MacRumors: iPad mini 60Hz OLED 소문 Apple Newsroom: iPhone Duo 사전 주문 및 출시일 자주 묻는 질문 Apple 10월 13일 이벤트는 공식 확정됐나요? 네.
10월 13일 공개가 예상되는 Apple 신제품은? 가장 유력한 예상은 스마트 홈 제품 3종입니다. 각 제품의 공식 발표와 최종 사양은 아직 공개되지 않았습니다.
Apple 월드와이드 마케팅 수석부사장 Greg Joswiak은 “Welcome home.

Mac mini 알루미늄 액세서리 ZEERA MacFrost Pro Mac mini 액티브 쿨러 30W TEC 냉각 CNC 알루미늄 OLED 모니터링 3가지 냉각 모드 M6 / M5 Pro / M4 제품 보기 ZEERA MacForge Gen3 CNC 알루미늄 Mac mini 케이스 Mac Pro 그릴 CNC 섀시 향상된 공기 흐름 SSD 확장 전면 포트 제품 보기 지금 살까, Apple의 10월 발표를 기다릴까?

Apple 기기에 추천 ZEERA MagTri Gen2: 액티브 쿨링 탑재 25W Qi2.2 접이식 MagSafe 충전기 ZEERA MagTri Gen2는 iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods를 위한 접이식 3-in-1 MagSafe 충전 액세서리입니다. 호환 iPhone에 최대 25W Qi2.2 무선 충전을 제공하며, 장시간 충전 시 열을 관리하는 액티브 쿨링 시스템을 갖췄습니다. 접으면 작아져 책상, 침대 옆, 여행지에서 Apple 기기 3대를 한 충전 스테이션에 정리할 수 있습니다. 지금 구매 2026년 10월 9일 업데이트. 아래에서는 공식 일정과 보도·예상 제품 정보를 구분해 설명합니다.
Bloomberg 보도를 정리한 10월 8일 MacRumors 기사에 따르면 미디어 체험 행사와 온라인 영상 발표가 함께 진행될 전망입니다. 시청 정보는 Apple Events 및 Apple 공식 채널에서 확인하세요. 초대장 시작 시간만으로 일반 공개 영상의 게시 시간을 확정할 수는 없습니다.

Apple HomePad: 완전히 새로운 스마트 홈 디스플레이? 흔히 ‘HomePad’로 불리는 Apple Home Hub는 홈 제어, FaceTime, 위젯, 개인 정보를 가족이 공유하는 디스플레이로서 가장 큰 신제품이 될 가능성이 있습니다. 보도에 따르면 약 6인치 화면, 벽걸이형과 스피커 베이스형, 가족 구성원에 맞춰 인터페이스를 바꾸는 카메라와 재실 센서를 갖춥니다. 약 350달러부터라는 전망이 있지만 Apple은 가격을 발표하지 않았습니다. 주방 캘린더, 복도 제어 화면, 가족용 통화 기기 등 실제 설치 위치를 생각해 보세요. 여러 대를 사기 전에 앱 지원, 계정 개인정보 보호, 설치 조건, 지원 언어를 확인해야 합니다.
Bloomberg 보도를 정리한 MacRumors 최신 기사 는 다음 공개 시점을 10월 27일 전후으로 봅니다. 이는 보도된 일정이며 Apple 공식 초대장이 아닙니다. 제품 변형에 따라 전체 수를 세는 방식도 달라질 수 있습니다.
Apple의 설명 전에는 휴대 사용, 전체 iPad App Store, 동일한 앱 호환성을 전제로 하지 마세요. 기존 HomePod도 같은 Siri AI 기능을 받나요? 기능별로 지원 여부가 다를 수 있습니다. 발표 후 Apple이 제시하는 지원 모델, 소프트웨어 버전, 언어, 지역을 확인하세요. iPad mini 8에 120Hz 화면이 탑재되나요?
HomePod 프로세서와 색상 전망은 제공된 영상 해설에도 나오지만 Apple의 공식 사양표는 아닙니다.
M6 iMac M6 iMac이 7번째 주목 제품군입니다. 영상은 대대적인 재설계보다 칩 중심 업데이트를 예상합니다. 데스크톱 구매 시 올인원인지, 컴퓨터와 모니터를 따로 살지 결정하세요.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple has set 13 October for a ‘Welcome home’ launch, and the rumours all point to smart home hardware.
In a post on X, Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, teased the company’s next reveal with a short video and four words: “Welcome home.
Invitations have also gone to some members of the press for an “Apple Experience” in Tribeca, New York, starting at 9:00 a.m.
ET on 13 October, as shared by Marques Brownlee .
9to5Mac notes that Apple ran a similar hands-on session for the MacBook Neo earlier this year.
Welcome home. October 13. pic.twitter.com/ChelGSDOTI
9to5Mac also expects the LG-made smart lock and thermostat that leaked recently to appear, since Apple reportedly co-developed them with LG.
MacRumors says the hub has been ready for months and was waiting on Siri AI, which TechRadar notes arrived last month with iOS 27.
The launch also follows our look at the three Apple launches to watch this month .
Apple hasn’t said where the products will go on sale, or at what price.
Pricing so far is a US rumour only, so there is no UAE figure to cite yet.
Everything below comes from rumours and code leaks, not Apple.

빠른 답변 Apple이 2026년 10월 13일 ‘Welcome home’ 신제품 공개를 공식 확인했습니다. 초대장에 따르면 뉴욕 트라이베카에서 Apple Experience가 열리며 시작 시간은 미국 동부시간 오전 9시. 주목할 제품은 신형 Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini 2, 그리고 HomePad로 불리는 스마트 홈 디스플레이입니다. 이후 10월 말에는 Mac과 iPad 4개 제품군이 추가 공개될 것으로 보도됐지만, 해당 라인업은 Apple이 확인하지 않았습니다. 구매를 미룰 수 있다면 Apple TV나 HomePod mini를 사기 전에 10월 13일 발표를 확인하세요.

October 13.” MacRumors: 10월 13일 제품 공개 공식 발표 MacRumors: 10월 13일 스마트 홈 프리뷰 MacRumors: 10월 말 MacBook Pro·iPad mini 공개 보도 MacRumors: iPad mini 60Hz OLED 소문 Apple Newsroom: iPhone Duo 사전 주문 및 출시일 자주 묻는 질문 Apple 10월 13일 이벤트는 공식 확정됐나요? 네.
10월 13일 공개가 예상되는 Apple 신제품은? 가장 유력한 예상은 스마트 홈 제품 3종입니다. 각 제품의 공식 발표와 최종 사양은 아직 공개되지 않았습니다.
Apple 월드와이드 마케팅 수석부사장 Greg Joswiak은 “Welcome home.

Mac mini 알루미늄 액세서리 ZEERA MacFrost Pro Mac mini 액티브 쿨러 30W TEC 냉각 CNC 알루미늄 OLED 모니터링 3가지 냉각 모드 M6 / M5 Pro / M4 제품 보기 ZEERA MacForge Gen3 CNC 알루미늄 Mac mini 케이스 Mac Pro 그릴 CNC 섀시 향상된 공기 흐름 SSD 확장 전면 포트 제품 보기 지금 살까, Apple의 10월 발표를 기다릴까?

Apple 기기에 추천 ZEERA MagTri Gen2: 액티브 쿨링 탑재 25W Qi2.2 접이식 MagSafe 충전기 ZEERA MagTri Gen2는 iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods를 위한 접이식 3-in-1 MagSafe 충전 액세서리입니다. 호환 iPhone에 최대 25W Qi2.2 무선 충전을 제공하며, 장시간 충전 시 열을 관리하는 액티브 쿨링 시스템을 갖췄습니다. 접으면 작아져 책상, 침대 옆, 여행지에서 Apple 기기 3대를 한 충전 스테이션에 정리할 수 있습니다. 지금 구매 2026년 10월 9일 업데이트. 아래에서는 공식 일정과 보도·예상 제품 정보를 구분해 설명합니다.
Bloomberg 보도를 정리한 10월 8일 MacRumors 기사에 따르면 미디어 체험 행사와 온라인 영상 발표가 함께 진행될 전망입니다. 시청 정보는 Apple Events 및 Apple 공식 채널에서 확인하세요. 초대장 시작 시간만으로 일반 공개 영상의 게시 시간을 확정할 수는 없습니다.

Apple HomePad: 완전히 새로운 스마트 홈 디스플레이? 흔히 ‘HomePad’로 불리는 Apple Home Hub는 홈 제어, FaceTime, 위젯, 개인 정보를 가족이 공유하는 디스플레이로서 가장 큰 신제품이 될 가능성이 있습니다. 보도에 따르면 약 6인치 화면, 벽걸이형과 스피커 베이스형, 가족 구성원에 맞춰 인터페이스를 바꾸는 카메라와 재실 센서를 갖춥니다. 약 350달러부터라는 전망이 있지만 Apple은 가격을 발표하지 않았습니다. 주방 캘린더, 복도 제어 화면, 가족용 통화 기기 등 실제 설치 위치를 생각해 보세요. 여러 대를 사기 전에 앱 지원, 계정 개인정보 보호, 설치 조건, 지원 언어를 확인해야 합니다.
Bloomberg 보도를 정리한 MacRumors 최신 기사 는 다음 공개 시점을 10월 27일 전후으로 봅니다. 이는 보도된 일정이며 Apple 공식 초대장이 아닙니다. 제품 변형에 따라 전체 수를 세는 방식도 달라질 수 있습니다.
Apple의 설명 전에는 휴대 사용, 전체 iPad App Store, 동일한 앱 호환성을 전제로 하지 마세요. 기존 HomePod도 같은 Siri AI 기능을 받나요? 기능별로 지원 여부가 다를 수 있습니다. 발표 후 Apple이 제시하는 지원 모델, 소프트웨어 버전, 언어, 지역을 확인하세요. iPad mini 8에 120Hz 화면이 탑재되나요?
HomePod 프로세서와 색상 전망은 제공된 영상 해설에도 나오지만 Apple의 공식 사양표는 아닙니다.
M6 iMac M6 iMac이 7번째 주목 제품군입니다. 영상은 대대적인 재설계보다 칩 중심 업데이트를 예상합니다. 데스크톱 구매 시 올인원인지, 컴퓨터와 모니터를 따로 살지 결정하세요.

Apple could be preparing to announce a new partnership with home security company ADT as part of its “Welcome home” product launch on Tuesday, October 13.
The Apple Post has rounded up everything expected from the event ahead of Tuesday’s announcements.
Stay up to date with real-time notifications, bookmark stories to read offline, and keep up with the latest headlines from the Home Screen widget.
Several of the new hires are also reportedly expecting to receive more information about their responsibilities later this month, potentially lining up with Apple’s October 13 announcements.
The most obvious role for ADT would be professional installation.
Apple is expected to introduce a wall-mounted version of HomePad, while the company is also reportedly working with LG on a wider ecosystem of connected-home products.
MacRumors says some ADT employees have been told the secretive role will involve home automation and in-home installation services.
That could give Apple a ready-made network of technicians able to install wall-mounted hubs and related accessories for customers who do not want to handle setup themselves.
It remains unclear whether any agreement would extend beyond installation into ADT’s home security monitoring services.

ADT already has a relationship with Google in the smart home market, although MacRumors reports that people familiar with the matter believe the agreement has either expired or is due to expire and is not expected to be renewed.
Apple today announced an upcoming product launch that will take place on Tuesday, October 13.
We are expecting Apple's announcement to focus on new smart home products, including the long-rumored smart home hub, a new Apple TV 4K, and a refreshed HomePod mini .
Attendees will likely get hands-on time with the new products Apple introduces.

Rumors suggest Apple has several Macs coming before the end of the year, but those could be introduced at later in the year instead of during the home product launch.

Apple HomePad: 완전히 새로운 스마트 홈 디스플레이? 흔히 ‘HomePad’로 불리는 Apple Home Hub는 홈 제어, FaceTime, 위젯, 개인 정보를 가족이 공유하는 디스플레이로서 가장 큰 신제품이 될 가능성이 있습니다. 보도에 따르면 약 6인치 화면, 벽걸이형과 스피커 베이스형, 가족 구성원에 맞춰 인터페이스를 바꾸는 카메라와 재실 센서를 갖춥니다. 약 350달러부터라는 전망이 있지만 Apple은 가격을 발표하지 않았습니다. 주방 캘린더, 복도 제어 화면, 가족용 통화 기기 등 실제 설치 위치를 생각해 보세요. 여러 대를 사기 전에 앱 지원, 계정 개인정보 보호, 설치 조건, 지원 언어를 확인해야 합니다.
Bloomberg 보도를 정리한 MacRumors 최신 기사 는 다음 공개 시점을 10월 27일 전후으로 봅니다. 이는 보도된 일정이며 Apple 공식 초대장이 아닙니다. 제품 변형에 따라 전체 수를 세는 방식도 달라질 수 있습니다.

sources.title: Apple confirms ‘Welcome home’ launch for 13 October, with smart home products expected - Tbreak UAE
passages: Apple has set 13 October for a ‘Welcome home’ launch, and the rumours all point to smart home hardware.
In a post on X, Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, teased the company’s next reveal with a short video and four words: “Welcome home.
Invitations have also gone to some members of the press for an “Apple Experience” in Tribeca, New York, starting at 9:00 a.m.
ET on 13 October, as shared by Marques Brownlee .
9to5Mac notes that Apple ran a similar hands-on session for the MacBook Neo earlier this year.
Welcome home. October 13. pic.twitter.com/ChelGSDOTI
9to5Mac also expects the LG-made smart lock and thermostat that leaked recently to appear, since Apple reportedly co-developed them with LG.
MacRumors says the hub has been ready for months and was waiting on Siri AI, which TechRadar notes arrived last month with iOS 27.
The launch also follows our look at the three Apple launches to watch this month .
Apple hasn’t said where the products will go on sale, or at what price.
Pricing so far is a US rumour only, so there is no UAE figure to cite yet.
Everything below comes from rumours and code leaks, not Apple.

extraction.body: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports. Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”. Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder .

Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection,” he said.(Also Read: Jobseeker nearly falls for AI-powered recruitment scam promising double salary: 'The usual red flags weren't there')His comparison highlights the difference between established consumer safety regulations and the evolving rules governing AI. Although artificial intelligence is already covered by laws in various countries, Smith believes more consistent requirements are needed to address risks posed by increasingly capable systems.He also called for companies to introduce “emergency brakes”, commonly known as kill switches, to pause or slow down AI systems if they begin behaving dangerously. Smith wants companies to prepare incident reports and ensure people are informed if rogue AI agents breach their systems.He described AI as both a “tool and a weapon”, arguing that stronger safeguards are urgently needed.What are the risks of rogue AI agents?AI agents can perform multi-step tasks using digital tools and websites with limited human intervention, raising concerns about unexpected behaviour and potential exploitation by malicious actors.Security is another concern. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK's AI Security Institute, warned about the risk of hostile countries stealing powerful AI models, according to The Guardian.The risks are not limited to cybersecurity. In an incident reported by the Associated Press, Anthropic's Claude AI submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder while performing tasks on a website. What could tougher AI regulation mean?Smith's comments come as the UK considers stronger oversight of advanced AI models. AI minister Kanishka Narayan is expected to urge companies developing frontier AI to improve safeguards, while the government prepares to legislate for greater oversight, according to the report.(Also Read: Canva co-founder Cameron Adams reveals what he learnt from failed Google Wave project)Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella has also called for better containment measures. In an October 10 post, reported by The Indian Express, Nadella argued that AI systems should be designed so their behaviour can be observed, their limits tested and their actions contained.The debate highlights the challenge of encouraging AI innovation while protecting public safety. Smith argues that voluntary promises are not enough, and stronger safety standards, security and accountability are needed to keep pace with AI's growing capabilities.

Smith made the comparison in a BBC interview published over the weekend, where he described AI as both a “tool and a weapon” that needs urgent oversight. “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI,” he said, according to the BBC. “Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” Smith is calling for a legal structure that would make AI companies more accountable when things go wrong from their products or end. Under his proposal, firms would have to report model failures, alert anyone whose systems are breached by a rogue AI agent, and submit powerful models to independent scrutiny before making them public. Smith’s push for legally enforceable AI safeguards puts him at odds with the White House. Trump has argued that the US should let its AI industry regulate itself , warning that tighter rules could leave the country behind China. President Trump reiterated that position at a summit with technology executives last month. The summit also saw executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta, Google and Elon Musk’s X sign a one-page agreement that Cryptopolitan described as “morally binding.” The signatories pledged to use independent auditors and put safeguards in place to prevent AI models from going rogue. Microsoft, however, did not sign this accord, according to The Telegraph. Smith welcomed the agreement and said Microsoft would be willing to sign it. But in an interview with the BBC, he cautioned that voluntary commitments alone would not go far enough. He called the agreement “a good step” and “a necessary step,” but added that he did not thik it was sufficient any longer. He warned that voluntary commitments may do little to curb the biggest risks, since companies that already take safety seriously are more likely to follow them, while those that pose the greatest danger can choose to ignore them. Microsoft’s President Smith also named the UK as the country best placed to set global standards and not the US or even Brussels. He pointed to its AI Security Institute , launched in 2024 under then prime minister Rishi Sunak as the AI Safety Institute. The body has secured voluntary agreements allowing it to test frontier models before they ship. According to Smith, the UK is in a stronger position than the EU when dealing with Washington, as US policymakers view London differently from Brussels, he told the BBC, adding that the EU’s risk-based AI Act has made US policymakers wary. The UK government is also preparing to tighten its oversight of AI, with AI minister Kanishka Narayan expected to call on developers of frontier models to do more to address safety risks in an upcoming speech, as legislation to strengthen government oversight continues to take shape. Separately, The Telegraph also reported that the White House had restored the UK institute’s access to the latest AI models for testing. The access had previously been withdrawn after firms including Anthropic and OpenAI were asked to stop sharing their models. extraction.body: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules for AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports. Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”. Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder .

Under his proposal, firms would have to report model failures, alert anyone whose systems are breached by a rogue AI agent, and submit powerful models to independent scrutiny before making them public. Smith’s push for legally enforceable AI safeguards puts him at odds with the White House. Trump has argued that the US should let its AI industry regulate itself , warning that tighter rules could leave the country behind China. President Trump reiterated that position at a summit with technology executives last month. The summit also saw executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta, Google and Elon Musk’s X sign a one-page agreement that Cryptopolitan described as “morally binding.” The signatories pledged to use independent auditors and put safeguards in place to prevent AI models from going rogue. Microsoft, however, did not sign this accord, according to The Telegraph. Smith welcomed the agreement and said Microsoft would be willing to sign it. But in an interview with the BBC, he cautioned that voluntary commitments alone would not go far enough. He called the agreement “a good step” and “a necessary step,” but added that he did not thik it was sufficient any longer. He warned that voluntary commitments may do little to curb the biggest risks, since companies that already take safety seriously are more likely to follow them, while those that pose the greatest danger can choose to ignore them. Microsoft’s President Smith also named the UK as the country best placed to set global standards and not the US or even Brussels. He pointed to its AI Security Institute , launched in 2024 under then prime minister Rishi Sunak as the AI Safety Institute. The body has secured voluntary agreements allowing it to test frontier models before they ship. According to Smith, the UK is in a stronger position than the EU when dealing with Washington, as US policymakers view London differently from Brussels, he told the BBC, adding that the EU’s risk-based AI Act has made US policymakers wary. The warnings follow real incidents, with Anthropic recently finding out that a version of its Claude model had contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder during testing. extraction.body: Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well. I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense. Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.” Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. What I’ve really liked about that is this sense of “No, you actually have to make the case for it.” You can’t just say, “This is the future, shut up.” And then specifically about Tesla and the abundance thing, what was shocking to me is not so much that they haven’t come up with a definition of abundance, but that that was a promise that they were making in the first place. I think [that] speaks to how strange our relationship to Tesla, and particularly the people who are invested and ride-or-die for Elon, [has become.] It’s not about, is this company going to sell a lot of cars? It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold.

sources.title: Demands for Data Center Moratoriums Surge - The American Prospect
passages: The major artificial intelligence companies’ prime directive to literally bulldoze AI infrastructure into states with minimal regulation has produced citizen-led, bipartisan demands for local and national moratoriums on data center siting.

While the Trump administration is doing everything it can to facilitate the only capital spending with a pulse in the economy, these calls for moratoriums are growing, and connecting with local successes in blocking data center construction.
Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers.
Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF.

A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined.

Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands.

The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs.

Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) recently called for a national moratorium on the construction of data centers that are “powering this unregulated sprint to develop and deploy AI.” Sanders did credit “the transformative power of AI and robotics” before calling out Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, and Bill Gates with a simple question: “Are these multibillionaires staying up nights worrying about what AI and robotics will do to the working families of our country and the world?” The answer would be mostly no. Over 230 organizations across the 50 states signed on to a letter to members of Congress organized by Food & Water Watch, a national advocacy group, also calling for a national moratorium on data center siting and construction. The letter characterized generative AI and crypto as generational threats. But it’s the local rejections of data centers—in places as varied as Chandler, Arizona , and Leesburg, Indiana —that should have the tech oligarchs worried. These results demonstrate that Americans are beginning to grasp the downsides of inserting AI into every facet of daily life. This mushrooming grassroots backlash promises to dominate American politics in 2026. The fallout from siting these gargantuan facilities near human habitats continues to convulse communities. Residential ratepayers are already grappling with electricity price spikes and see data centers as a major driver of the pain. Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF. A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined. “Electricity is the new price of eggs,” one industry analyst told The New York Times , and if you’re concerned about electricity, you have to be concerned about data centers. Since 2019, at least 40 states—both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Data centers are also guzzling city-sized amounts of water. By 2028, they’ll require up to 720 billion gallons of water every year to keep servers cool—usage would fill one million Olympic-size swimming pools or furnish water for the interior-home uses of 18.5 million American households. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious. Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands. Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river. DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public. Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle. Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through. That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident. The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.” Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium. SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks. President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion. The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.” Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebecca Bellan, and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one-year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms of how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried. It’s also noteworthy that Microsoft, earlier this year, made a similar announcement about not using NDAs. I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it. I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step. Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right? This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc. And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant. But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them. And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well. I wrote a story last week about how it’s been a year since we’ve really heard Tesla beating its own drum about building towards what it originally was calling “sustainable abundance” and is now “amazing abundance” as its mission statement. It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was. It read like LLM nonsense. Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.” Obviously that future is barreling ahead in a lot of ways, but in a few key ways, there have been these obstacles. It’s about this vision for remaking society. Or at least, that’s what they’re being sold.
