extraction.body: The major artificial intelligence companies’ prime directive to literally bulldoze AI infrastructure into states with minimal regulation has produced citizen-led, bipartisan demands for local and national moratoriums on data center siting. While the Trump administration is doing everything it can to facilitate the only capital spending with a pulse in the economy, these calls for moratoriums are growing, and connecting with local successes in blocking data center construction. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) recently called for a national moratorium on the construction of data centers that are “powering this unregulated sprint to develop and deploy AI.” Sanders did credit “the transformative power of AI and robotics” before calling out Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, and Bill Gates with a simple question: “Are these multibillionaires staying up nights worrying about what AI and robotics will do to the working families of our country and the world?” The answer would be mostly no. Over 230 organizations across the 50 states signed on to a letter to members of Congress organized by Food & Water Watch, a national advocacy group, also calling for a national moratorium on data center siting and construction. The letter characterized generative AI and crypto as generational threats. But it’s the local rejections of data centers—in places as varied as Chandler, Arizona , and Leesburg, Indiana —that should have the tech oligarchs worried. These results demonstrate that Americans are beginning to grasp the downsides of inserting AI into every facet of daily life. This mushrooming grassroots backlash promises to dominate American politics in 2026. The fallout from siting these gargantuan facilities near human habitats continues to convulse communities. Residential ratepayers are already grappling with electricity price spikes and see data centers as a major driver of the pain. Power demand from data centers will hit 106 gigawatts by 2035 , according to an analysis from BloombergNEF. A Yale Clean Energy Forum report estimates that data centers could take up as much as 12 percent of total U.S. power consumption by 2028, a higher demand than all manufacturing of steel, aluminum, and other high-intensity manufactured goods combined. “Electricity is the new price of eggs,” one industry analyst told The New York Times , and if you’re concerned about electricity, you have to be concerned about data centers. Since 2019, at least 40 states—both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Data centers are also guzzling city-sized amounts of water. By 2028, they’ll require up to 720 billion gallons of water every year to keep servers cool—usage would fill one million Olympic-size swimming pools or furnish water for the interior-home uses of 18.5 million American households. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious. Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands. Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river. DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public. Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle. Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through. That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident. The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.” Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium. SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms. Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks. President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion. The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.” Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. But despite their best efforts, local initiatives to stop the plowing over of homes and farms and businesses with giant warehouses of servers and chips will continue—and they’re starting to have an impact on the AI transition. The reason we can write these stories—stories that are orienting and informing rather than fear-inducing—is because of you. We removed programmatic ads from our site in April , which means that we don’t chase clicks for ad dollars. We don’t have a paywall, which means that everyone, regardless of their ability to pay, can access our work for free. We don’t have content partnerships with AI giants . We’re in our fall fundraising drive, and we need to raise $100,000 to hit our budget. We’re a nonprofit newsroom whose ability to write and report these stories depends on our readers. You are at the center of all of our decision making, from what we write to how we run our business. But this only works if the people who read and value our work step up to support us. We’re in our fall fundraising drive, and we need to raise $100,000 to hit our budget. We’re a nonprofit newsroom whose ability to write and report these stories depends on our readers. You are at the center of all of our decision making, from what we write to how we run our business. But this only works if the people who read and value our work step up to support us. Gabrielle Gurley is an American Prospect senior editor. The award-winning journalist covers politics and policy in states and localities, with beats in economic development and infrastructure, elections, and climate. She is a 2026 Society of Professional Journalists/Washington D.C. Chapter Correspondent Award finalist for her coverage of District of Columbia politics and has earned past recognitions from the National Association of Black Journalists and the Association for Education in Journalism and Mass Communication. In Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the region that represents the world’s largest data hub, data center expansions have collided with the climate crisis, leading to scrambles from local government to address the “ negative impacts on neighborhoods .” While the county wants to find environmental solutions that would reduce the burden on residents while still building the data centers, local elections in Loudoun County and throughout Virginia in November saw candidates who rejected data centers emerging victorious.

Even residents in the fresh water–rich Great Lakes states have raised questions about increased data center usage. Illinois also has one of the highest concentrations of data centers in the country, and local officials and environmentalists have raised alarms that siting decisions don’t always take into consideration how local drinking water needs can clash with data center cooling demands.

Georgia, Alabama, and Florida have actually had “ water wars .” In April, a federal judge ruled against Alabama in a dispute with Georgia over Army Corps of Engineers water allocations to metro Atlanta from Lake Allatoona, a northwest Georgia reservoir. Data center projects could complicate those interstate dynamics. NPR affiliate WABE reported that Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, which monitors the river running from North Georgia through Atlanta to Florida, tracks water usage plans for new data centers in the region. One facility , Coweta County’s Project Sail, would use nearly ten million gallons daily, which adds up to one-third of the county’s daily usage from the river.

DATA CENTER DEVELOPERS have been exceptionally skilled at persuading local leaders of their value to communities by touting gains like temporary construction jobs. (There are few on-site permanent jobs.) Unlike what’s transpired in Northern Virginia, where county officials hand out tax credits but still haul in millions in tax revenues, some recent data center projects are steering away from generous agreements with local communities. Instead, project officials focus on tax credits, obscure the details, force officials to sign nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and never divulge their supernova clients to the public.

Most residents are hard-pressed to fight corporate secrecy. The New York Times recently spotlighted Doña Ana County, New Mexico, a predominantly Latino community of 15,000. The data center developer for Project Jupiter, a multibillion-dollar component of the $500 billion SoftBank- and OpenAI-led Stargate Project, got to know the locals, but the underlying clients remained unknown because county officials had signed NDAs. Residents only found out after the project moved forward that the heavy hitters included OpenAI and Oracle.

Instead of property tax revenues, the county will see a payment in lieu of taxes (PILOT) program, which essentially allow companies to decide how much—or how little—money they’re willing to offer a community. But this trick isn’t having much staying power. Data Center Watch, coordinated by 10a Labs, an applied research and technology company specializing in AI security, reports that in the second quarter of 2025, data center opponents slowed the roll or thwarted projects totaling about $100 billion—more than the total of every quarter since 2023. In one three-month period, 20 projects fell through.

That includes a project in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, where Arizona’s former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema personally lobbied at local meetings for a 422,000-square-foot data center plan operated by Active Infrastructure, a hyperscale data center developer. In the end, the Chandler City Council voted against the data center unanimously . In rural Leesburg, Indiana, the town council refused to rezone land for industrial use to build a data center on 554 acres. “I’m really just trying to speak out for the future of agriculture, and passing a data center is not the future of agriculture,” said one local resident.

The possibility that a facility might be rejected has affected data center financing. In Michigan, Blue Owl Capital, a private credit firm, pulled out of a $10 billion data center deal with Oracle amid “shifting market sentiment around enormous AI spending” and concerns that “the Saline Township site … might face delays.”

Elsewhere in Michigan, data center opponents rallied in Lansing last week and called for “ no secret deals ” between local governments, utilities, and data center developers. At the gathering, Attorney General Dana Nessel demanded that the state’s public utility commission step back from fast-tracking a major utility project to power the Saline Township project. Anthony Hudson, a Republican gubernatorial candidate who attended the protest, mostly agreed with Nessel. A pair of state lawmakers, one a Democrat and the other a Republican, have teamed up to propose reversing tax breaks for large data center facilities. But residents want a statewide moratorium.
SINCE 2019, AT LEAST 40 STATES —both Republican and Democratic—have passed nearly 150 laws aiming to regulate AI and address known harms.

Unfortunately, federal regulation has lagged miles behind the internet revolution. The Senate did manage to stave off , by a vote of 99-to-1, a White House–endorsed attempt to prohibit states from passing AI regulations for ten years. The prohibition on state AI regulation came up again in the annual defense policy bill and was again beaten back. But even though that proposal generated outrage, the major overstep into state regulatory authority hasn’t motivated Republicans to fill in the blanks.

President Trump has seized on that inertia to issue more than half a dozen AI executive orders this year, the latest coming in mid-December complete with plans for a litigation task force and an annual evaluation of state laws determined to obliterate any opposition to AI usage or data center expansion.

The Brennan Center has labeled that move “little more than political theater.” Executive orders do not invest the federal government with the powers to file lawsuits. So federal officials cannot “directly enforce” the order through court action. “To challenge a state AI regulation in court,” writes Gowri Ramachandran, the director of elections and security in the center’s elections and government program, “the department would need to base the lawsuit on a federal statute or constitutional provision—not simply on the executive order itself.”

Combine data center moratorium drama with the gutting of the Affordable Care Act, the nothing-to-see-here response to the affordability crisis, and extortionate trade tactics, and the White House and congressional Republicans have set themselves and everyone else up for a very dismal New Year. But despite their best efforts, local initiatives to stop the plowing over of homes and farms and businesses with giant warehouses of servers and chips will continue—and they’re starting to have an impact on the AI transition.

extraction.body: Inside those buildings, which total half a million square feet together, is a massive construction project that’s still in progress. Once completed, it will house GM’s new Battery Cell Development Center, where the automaker is working furiously to build new prototype cells with the goal of slashing the cost of its EVs. Those EVs will have to compete not only with longtime sales leader Tesla, but also with the flood of Chinese EVs that, sooner or later, will land in the US. And while EV sales in the US appear to be leveling out, America has a long way to go before it can credibly compete with China, the world’s leading EV market. The number of shoppers interested in new and used EVs spiked when gas prices rose 40 percent this year as a result of the war in Iran — but mostly in models priced lower than the average $50,000 cost of a new vehicle today. While GM sells more EVs in the US than any other company after Tesla, most of its lineup is still too expensive thanks to a battery pack that makes up 30 to 40 percent of the total cost. During an early September tour, after putting on a hard hat, safety glasses, and a hi-vis vest, I saw up close the tools GM will use to build these newer, cheaper batteries: huge vats for mixing cell slurry, coating machines that deposit electrode material onto film, and machines for a dozen other steps in the process of turning minerals into cells that hold and deliver energy. The plant I toured will be a low-volume factory that lets engineers prototype the higher-volume production to come from giant, billion-dollar factories. The new facility suggests GM is playing a long game, working to develop new cells that use less — or none — of the minerals China controls globally. Although US scientists developed the original R&D on most new cell chemistries, Asian companies were the ones to develop, refine, and put those chemistries into volume production. The 15-year Chinese effort that gave the country global control of supply and processing for minerals used in today’s cells, especially cobalt, nickel, and rare earths, means future cells must use different minerals to escape the country’s dominance. A second: This spring GM announced it’s working with startup Peak Energy on sodium-ion cells for energy storage. China may already be selling its EVs to Americans by then. The company’s battery engineers are confident that using the new facility inside those anonymous buildings 15 miles north of Detroit can launch new cell chemistries and formats for EVs and battery energy-storage systems in less time than predicted. BCDC head Mo Gallegos puts the total cost at $900 million. Inside the 500,000-square-foot lab, I saw much of the machinery needed to fabricate a cell, from mixing slurry for the coating that forms a cell electrode to the charging hardware that energizes a finished cell for the first time. The mini factory will be used for multiple cell chemistries and different formats, starting with prismatic cells. Its purpose is to test industrial cell manufacturing processes, proving and optimizing production techniques and recipes before they’re implemented at scale. While the BCDC will produce actual working cells, it will do so in far lower volumes and at slower speeds than the production lines at full-scale cell plants. GM’s battery developers will then transfer the knowledge gained from this process testing to its cell production partners that will take the new designs to full-scale volume. Those would likely include the two plants operated by Ultium Cells LLC, the joint cell production venture between GM and its cell partner, LG Energy Solution. The second, in Spring Hills, Tennessee, opened in early 2024 and now produces lithium-ion phosphate cells for battery energy storage. Of the two BCDC buildings, the first houses anode and cathode fabrication on opposite sides, with electrode assembly in the middle. A bridge transports rolls of electrode film to the second building, where the cells are assembled, charged, and tested for eight to 11 days. Taking them all the way through development to commercialization means understanding how to build them; that requires testing production processes and methods to ensure the quality of the finished cells as well as their quantity. You can think of getting a cell to market in four phases: creating a new chemistry, testing early prototypes, figuring out how to build it, and then ramping up volume production. It created and tested new chemistries and cells for the pioneering EV1, the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, and the LMR chemistry the company plans to launch in 2028. But it’s limited to proving out a chemistry one cell at a time, in “coin” or small pouch formats. GM brought the second phase in-house when it opened its Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center in 2023. It will use real-world cell fabrication and battery assembly machinery to build thousands of cells a day — ideally assuring the ultimate ramp-up in a bigger plant goes smoothly. And it’s been built with double the floor space used initially to allow for future expansion, multiple chemistries, and multiple cell formats. Historically, those second and third phases were done by battery manufacturers. Wallace and the BCDC together give GM almost 1 million square feet of battery development space. (GM declined to specify how many employees worked at either facility, saying it varied.) The fourth and last phase is commercial production at scale, whether at Ultium Cells or other high-volume plants. To compare the scale of each phase, Kettering R&D might produce 1 liter of slurry with which to coat electrode film to test individual cells. The Wallace lab takes that to 40 liters at a time. Agility in developing and refining new designs fast comes from using “digital twins” to simulate processes well before production hardware enters the process, said Radu Theyyunni, GM’s director of virtual engineering for global propulsion.

extraction.body:
This article was published more than 6 years ago. Some information may no longer be current. An worker tests the charging port of a Chevrolet Bolt at General Motors's Orion plant in Michigan. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail At the General Motors plant in Lake Orion, Mich., two workers put a gas tank into a Chevrolet Sonic in just over a minute. Then an eerily-silent automated electric cart sped across the floor to deliver a battery for the next car on the line – an all-electric Chevy Bolt. The same two workers attached the Bolt’s battery in the same time it took them to put in the Sonic’s gas tank. Then another Sonic rolled up, needing a gas tank. This was in March, just before the COVID-19 pandemic shut U.S. car-manufacturing plants, including Orion , for two months. The plant, which reopened this week, shows that workers building electric vehicles (EVs) can be the same people who build gas ones. Since 2016, this plant has built both the Bolt and gas-powered Sonic. Could GM’s electric move keep Elon Musk awake at night? At every station on the line, each worker – there are over 1,000 here – are also trained to work on either car. “Sometimes there are a bunch of Bolts in a row – it really depends on the orders we get,” said Jack Hund, GM’s EV/AV plant launch manager. After Orion was opened by U.S. President Ronald Reagan in 1984, the plant made sedans, including the Cadillac Fleetwood and, later, the Chevrolet Malibu. It was shut in 2009 when GM declared bankruptcy. But thanks to thanks to US$1-billion in grants and tax incentives, it reopened in 2011 and started building the Sonic. Electric cars are set to rescue another Michigan GM plant. Hamtramck, which made the Chevy Impala, was slated to close permanently along with four other North American plants in 2019. But in January, GM announced that it would spend US$2.2-billion to refit the plant to produce electric vehicles , including a Hummer pickup truck that, before COVID-19, was supposed to launch next year. It’s still unclear how many people that plant will employ when it’s operational. An EV battery destined for a Chevy Bolt sits on a trolley at the Orion plant. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail GM says it plans to sell 1 million EVs a year by 2025. In March, it revealed 10 concept EVs , most of them larger SUVs. The gradual shift to EVs is a long-term bid to save GM from sluggish sales and more plant closures. Other electric car makers have reopened shuttered automotive plants in the U.S. In 2010, Tesla took over a factory in Fremont, Calif., that had been built by GM decades earlier. Likewise, startup Rivian is spending US$750 million to convert a former Mitsubishi factory in Normal, Ill., into an electric truck factory. The shutdowns have hammered the auto industry overall, but electric cars might fare better than gas cars. Cheap gas and the shaky economy are expected to translate to 18-per-cent fewer EV sales than last year, but that’s still better than the 24-per-cent drop expected for gas cars , according to analyst Bloomberg NEF. Bloomberg NEF’s new report predicts that EV demand will rise in the long term, with electric cars counting for 58 per cent of new cars sold by 2040. That would mean 54 million EVs sold a year. EVs count only for a small fraction of sales right now, but Bloomberg predicts sales to rise from 1.7 million in 2020 to 8.5 million by 2025 as demand increases in Europe and China, batteries get cheaper and more charging infrastructure gets built. A Chevy Bolt moves down the line at the Orion plant. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail By the start of the next decade, EV sales could hit 26 million. That move could happen even faster if governments push EV manufacturing in their post-COVID recovery plans. In France, French Environment Minister Elisabeth Borne said the government will expand subsidies for electric cars as part of a plan to help the auto industry weather the downturn caused by COVID-19. Although that kind of government support for EVs is unlikely under the current U.S. administration, GM says it’s sticking to its plans, despite an 86-per-cent drop in net income during the lockdown. “We understand the seriousness of the business actions we have taken,” GM Chairman Mary Barra said in a call with analysts this month. “We will continue to [commit to EVs] because that’s what we think is the right thing to do for the future.” Authors and topics you follow will be added to your personal news feed in Following . © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. extraction.body: Inside those buildings, which total half a million square feet together, is a massive construction project that’s still in progress. Once completed, it will house GM’s new Battery Cell Development Center, where the automaker is working furiously to build new prototype cells with the goal of slashing the cost of its EVs. Those EVs will have to compete not only with longtime sales leader Tesla, but also with the flood of Chinese EVs that, sooner or later, will land in the US. And while EV sales in the US appear to be leveling out, America has a long way to go before it can credibly compete with China, the world’s leading EV market. The number of shoppers interested in new and used EVs spiked when gas prices rose 40 percent this year as a result of the war in Iran — but mostly in models priced lower than the average $50,000 cost of a new vehicle today. While GM sells more EVs in the US than any other company after Tesla, most of its lineup is still too expensive thanks to a battery pack that makes up 30 to 40 percent of the total cost. During an early September tour, after putting on a hard hat, safety glasses, and a hi-vis vest, I saw up close the tools GM will use to build these newer, cheaper batteries: huge vats for mixing cell slurry, coating machines that deposit electrode material onto film, and machines for a dozen other steps in the process of turning minerals into cells that hold and deliver energy. The plant I toured will be a low-volume factory that lets engineers prototype the higher-volume production to come from giant, billion-dollar factories. The new facility suggests GM is playing a long game, working to develop new cells that use less — or none — of the minerals China controls globally. Although US scientists developed the original R&D on most new cell chemistries, Asian companies were the ones to develop, refine, and put those chemistries into volume production. The 15-year Chinese effort that gave the country global control of supply and processing for minerals used in today’s cells, especially cobalt, nickel, and rare earths, means future cells must use different minerals to escape the country’s dominance. A second: This spring GM announced it’s working with startup Peak Energy on sodium-ion cells for energy storage. China may already be selling its EVs to Americans by then. The company’s battery engineers are confident that using the new facility inside those anonymous buildings 15 miles north of Detroit can launch new cell chemistries and formats for EVs and battery energy-storage systems in less time than predicted. BCDC head Mo Gallegos puts the total cost at $900 million. Inside the 500,000-square-foot lab, I saw much of the machinery needed to fabricate a cell, from mixing slurry for the coating that forms a cell electrode to the charging hardware that energizes a finished cell for the first time. The mini factory will be used for multiple cell chemistries and different formats, starting with prismatic cells. Its purpose is to test industrial cell manufacturing processes, proving and optimizing production techniques and recipes before they’re implemented at scale. While the BCDC will produce actual working cells, it will do so in far lower volumes and at slower speeds than the production lines at full-scale cell plants. GM’s battery developers will then transfer the knowledge gained from this process testing to its cell production partners that will take the new designs to full-scale volume. Those would likely include the two plants operated by Ultium Cells LLC, the joint cell production venture between GM and its cell partner, LG Energy Solution. The second, in Spring Hills, Tennessee, opened in early 2024 and now produces lithium-ion phosphate cells for battery energy storage. Of the two BCDC buildings, the first houses anode and cathode fabrication on opposite sides, with electrode assembly in the middle. A bridge transports rolls of electrode film to the second building, where the cells are assembled, charged, and tested for eight to 11 days. Taking them all the way through development to commercialization means understanding how to build them; that requires testing production processes and methods to ensure the quality of the finished cells as well as their quantity. You can think of getting a cell to market in four phases: creating a new chemistry, testing early prototypes, figuring out how to build it, and then ramping up volume production. It created and tested new chemistries and cells for the pioneering EV1, the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, and the LMR chemistry the company plans to launch in 2028. But it’s limited to proving out a chemistry one cell at a time, in “coin” or small pouch formats. GM brought the second phase in-house when it opened its Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center in 2023. It will use real-world cell fabrication and battery assembly machinery to build thousands of cells a day — ideally assuring the ultimate ramp-up in a bigger plant goes smoothly. And it’s been built with double the floor space used initially to allow for future expansion, multiple chemistries, and multiple cell formats. Historically, those second and third phases were done by battery manufacturers. Wallace and the BCDC together give GM almost 1 million square feet of battery development space. (GM declined to specify how many employees worked at either facility, saying it varied.) The fourth and last phase is commercial production at scale, whether at Ultium Cells or other high-volume plants. To compare the scale of each phase, Kettering R&D might produce 1 liter of slurry with which to coat electrode film to test individual cells. The Wallace lab takes that to 40 liters at a time. Agility in developing and refining new designs fast comes from using “digital twins” to simulate processes well before production hardware enters the process, said Radu Theyyunni, GM’s director of virtual engineering for global propulsion.

extraction.body:
This article was published more than 6 years ago. Some information may no longer be current. An worker tests the charging port of a Chevrolet Bolt at General Motors's Orion plant in Michigan. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail At the General Motors plant in Lake Orion, Mich., two workers put a gas tank into a Chevrolet Sonic in just over a minute. Then an eerily-silent automated electric cart sped across the floor to deliver a battery for the next car on the line – an all-electric Chevy Bolt. The same two workers attached the Bolt’s battery in the same time it took them to put in the Sonic’s gas tank. Then another Sonic rolled up, needing a gas tank. This was in March, just before the COVID-19 pandemic shut U.S. car-manufacturing plants, including Orion , for two months. The plant, which reopened this week, shows that workers building electric vehicles (EVs) can be the same people who build gas ones. Since 2016, this plant has built both the Bolt and gas-powered Sonic. Could GM’s electric move keep Elon Musk awake at night? At every station on the line, each worker – there are over 1,000 here – are also trained to work on either car. “Sometimes there are a bunch of Bolts in a row – it really depends on the orders we get,” said Jack Hund, GM’s EV/AV plant launch manager. After Orion was opened by U.S. President Ronald Reagan in 1984, the plant made sedans, including the Cadillac Fleetwood and, later, the Chevrolet Malibu. It was shut in 2009 when GM declared bankruptcy. But thanks to thanks to US$1-billion in grants and tax incentives, it reopened in 2011 and started building the Sonic. Electric cars are set to rescue another Michigan GM plant. Hamtramck, which made the Chevy Impala, was slated to close permanently along with four other North American plants in 2019. But in January, GM announced that it would spend US$2.2-billion to refit the plant to produce electric vehicles , including a Hummer pickup truck that, before COVID-19, was supposed to launch next year. It’s still unclear how many people that plant will employ when it’s operational. An EV battery destined for a Chevy Bolt sits on a trolley at the Orion plant. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail GM says it plans to sell 1 million EVs a year by 2025. In March, it revealed 10 concept EVs , most of them larger SUVs. The gradual shift to EVs is a long-term bid to save GM from sluggish sales and more plant closures. Other electric car makers have reopened shuttered automotive plants in the U.S. In 2010, Tesla took over a factory in Fremont, Calif., that had been built by GM decades earlier. Likewise, startup Rivian is spending US$750 million to convert a former Mitsubishi factory in Normal, Ill., into an electric truck factory. The shutdowns have hammered the auto industry overall, but electric cars might fare better than gas cars. Cheap gas and the shaky economy are expected to translate to 18-per-cent fewer EV sales than last year, but that’s still better than the 24-per-cent drop expected for gas cars , according to analyst Bloomberg NEF. Bloomberg NEF’s new report predicts that EV demand will rise in the long term, with electric cars counting for 58 per cent of new cars sold by 2040. That would mean 54 million EVs sold a year. EVs count only for a small fraction of sales right now, but Bloomberg predicts sales to rise from 1.7 million in 2020 to 8.5 million by 2025 as demand increases in Europe and China, batteries get cheaper and more charging infrastructure gets built. A Chevy Bolt moves down the line at the Orion plant. Jason Tchir/The Globe and Mail By the start of the next decade, EV sales could hit 26 million. That move could happen even faster if governments push EV manufacturing in their post-COVID recovery plans. In France, French Environment Minister Elisabeth Borne said the government will expand subsidies for electric cars as part of a plan to help the auto industry weather the downturn caused by COVID-19. Although that kind of government support for EVs is unlikely under the current U.S. administration, GM says it’s sticking to its plans, despite an 86-per-cent drop in net income during the lockdown. “We understand the seriousness of the business actions we have taken,” GM Chairman Mary Barra said in a call with analysts this month. “We will continue to [commit to EVs] because that’s what we think is the right thing to do for the future.” Authors and topics you follow will be added to your personal news feed in Following . © Copyright 2026 The Globe and Mail Inc. All rights reserved.

But thanks to thanks to US$1-billion in grants and tax incentives, it reopened in 2011 and started building the Sonic.
Electric cars are set to rescue another Michigan GM plant.

Hamtramck, which made the Chevy Impala, was slated to close permanently along with four other North American plants in 2019. Other electric car makers have reopened shuttered automotive plants in the U.S. In 2010, Tesla took over a factory in Fremont, Calif., that had been built by GM decades earlier. “However, the key to getting updates from Windows Update beyond 2027 is to keep your devices up to date today,” Microsoft’s Andrew Brown said .
Microsoft is advising users and businesses to update Windows devices before digital certificates used to verify Windows Update servers expire in May and June 2027.
Version 24H2 needs the September 2025 security update or a later release.
Supported systems that have fallen behind need the required security update.
Devices receiving updates through Windows Server Update Services, or WSUS, are excluded from this change.
Most users running a supported Windows version and installing monthly updates should receive the replacement certificates automatically.

passages: Microsoft has once again extended its Windows 10 licence - support will now end on 12 October 2027.
Official support for Windows 10 ended on 14 October 2025, unless you took action and extended your licence.
But ESU could provide you with a useful way to bridge the gap and keep using Windows 10 safely.
But the tech firm has now extended it for yet another year.
Meaning Microsoft will no longer offer fixes or security updates after that date (unless it extends it again) and your Windows 10 PC will be vulnerable to hackers.
Below this, you'll see an Enrol now link - click this.
Below, our tech experts run through next steps, including how to extend security support until October 2027.
Plus, we've included advice on what specs to look for if you're shopping for a new laptop or desktop PC.
Initially, Microsoft told its users they would have to pay if they wanted the one-year Windows licence extension.
In a Windows Experience Blog Update (24 June 2025), Microsoft outlined the two additional free options.
It also said the licence would be for one year only, taking you up to October 2026.
Hackers and criminals often target unsupported software to exploit weaknesses and steal data.
For PCs eligible for Windows 11, this includes the option to upgrade for free.
You can extend your licence until 13 October 2027.
We recommend doing this as it will keep your data safe and your PC running smoothly.
You need to have the latest version of Windows 10 in order for this to work.
Click Start > Settings > Update & Security , then click Check for updates .
Our own research* suggests that the equivalent of around 21million people in the UK own and use a PC running Windows 10.
Windows 11 feels similar to Windows 10 and it’s actually been simplified to make it easier to use.
8% of Which? members who have Windows 10 told us** they plan on paying somebody to upgrade their PC.
Enrolment in ESU isn’t automatic, so you’ll need to take action to remain safe.
Microsoft is currently rolling out a prompt to begin the enrolment process via Windows Update.
You can enrol for free if you agree to back up your Windows settings to the cloud.
In each case, you should now see a screen confirming that your device has been enrolled to receive extended security updates until October 13 2026.
Windows updates make sure your PC stays secure through security updates and the latest fixes, so it continues to run properly and stay protected.
We suggest installing Windows 11 sooner rather than later, so make sure you take advantage of Microsoft's offer while it lasts.
Chromebooks run ChromeOS, which works differently from Windows: it has an online focus and needs you to have a Google account.
You do all your tasks online via your browser or through apps downloaded from the Google Play Store.
If you mainly use online apps, such as Google’s own Docs and Sheets, a Chromebook could suit you well.
Also, many popular apps, including Microsoft Office, are available to download or buy.
However, Windows software isn't compatible – so some programs may not be available.

Microsoft has once again extended its Windows 10 licence - support will now end on 12 October 2027. Official support for Windows 10 ended on 14 October 2025, unless you took action and extended your licence.

Originally, if you had extended your licence, Microsoft had said your support would end on 13 October 2026. But the tech firm has now extended it for yet another year. Meaning Microsoft will no longer offer fixes or security updates after that date (unless it extends it again) and your Windows 10 PC will be vulnerable to hackers.
If you have a Windows 10 PC, you’ve likely already have seen notifications informing you about the end of support. For PCs eligible for Windows 11, this includes the option to upgrade for free.

Not all PCs with Windows 10 will have the necessary specs to upgrade, though. And if you have a PC running Windows 7 or 8.1 (or one bought with these and later upgraded to Windows 10), you almost certainly won't.

Below, our tech experts run through next steps, including how to extend security support until October 2027. Plus, we've included advice on what specs to look for if you're shopping for a new laptop or desktop PC.

Windows updates make sure your PC stays secure through security updates and the latest fixes, so it continues to run properly and stay protected.

Windows 10 will still function even though support has ended – but it won’t get security updates unless you take action. Hackers and criminals often target unsupported software to exploit weaknesses and steal data. You might also find over time that some features or software will no longer work on your PC.
Anyone using Windows 10 on their PC will be affected. Our own research* suggests that the equivalent of around 21million people in the UK own and use a PC running Windows 10.
You can extend your licence until 13 October 2027. We recommend doing this as it will keep your data safe and your PC running smoothly. Then upgrade when you can.

If your machine isn't eligible to upgrade, you can buy a new computer (see below). Alternatively, if you have a desktop PC, you could upgrade outdated components .

If you’re reluctant to fork out for a new PC, consider whether converting your Windows laptop to a Chromebook is right for you. ChromeOS Flex is free to install and has much lighter requirements than Windows 11, so it’s likely to be compatible with your older device.

You do all your tasks online via your browser or through apps downloaded from the Google Play Store. If you mainly use online apps, such as Google’s own Docs and Sheets, a Chromebook could suit you well.
Also, many popular apps, including Microsoft Office, are available to download or buy. However, Windows software isn't compatible – so some programs may not be available.

Ultimately, if you want to continue to use Windows, you’ll need to switch to Windows 11 at some point between now and 12 October 2027. But ESU could provide you with a useful way to bridge the gap and keep using Windows 10 safely.

Enrolment in ESU isn’t automatic, so you’ll need to take action to remain safe. Microsoft is currently rolling out a prompt to begin the enrolment process via Windows Update. There are several ways to qualify for ESU. You can enrol for free if you agree to back up your Windows settings to the cloud. Otherwise, you can redeem Microsoft loyalty points (if you have earned any), or pay a one-off fee.

Microsoft is advising users and businesses to update Windows devices before digital certificates used to verify Windows Update servers expire in May and June 2027. The certificates expire on May 17 or June 19, depending on the Windows version. Devices without replacement certificates will lose access to Windows Update, including security fixes delivered through the service. Microsoft is distributing the replacements through a process known as certificate rotation. “However, the key to getting updates from Windows Update beyond 2027 is to keep your devices up to date today,” Microsoft’s Andrew Brown said . Supported systems that have fallen behind need the required security update. Microsoft advises users with unsupported versions to upgrade. Windows 11 version 25H2 and later require no action. Version 24H2 needs the September 2025 security update or a later release. Several other supported versions need the July 2026 update or later. Supported systems can regain access after the deadline by installing the required update. Administrators can download it from the Microsoft Update Catalog or distribute it through their management tools. Devices receiving updates through Windows Server Update Services, or WSUS, are excluded from this change.

You need to have the latest version of Windows 10 in order for this to work.
Click Start > Settings > Update & Security , then click Check for updates .
Our own research* suggests that the equivalent of around 21million people in the UK own and use a PC running Windows 10.
Windows 11 feels similar to Windows 10 and it’s actually been simplified to make it easier to use.
8% of Which? members who have Windows 10 told us** they plan on paying somebody to upgrade their PC.
Enrolment in ESU isn’t automatic, so you’ll need to take action to remain safe.
Microsoft is currently rolling out a prompt to begin the enrolment process via Windows Update.
You can enrol for free if you agree to back up your Windows settings to the cloud.
In each case, you should now see a screen confirming that your device has been enrolled to receive extended security updates until October 13 2026.
Windows updates make sure your PC stays secure through security updates and the latest fixes, so it continues to run properly and stay protected.
We suggest installing Windows 11 sooner rather than later, so make sure you take advantage of Microsoft's offer while it lasts.
Chromebooks run ChromeOS, which works differently from Windows: it has an online focus and needs you to have a Google account.
You do all your tasks online via your browser or through apps downloaded from the Google Play Store.
If you mainly use online apps, such as Google’s own Docs and Sheets, a Chromebook could suit you well.
Also, many popular apps, including Microsoft Office, are available to download or buy.
However, Windows software isn't compatible – so some programs may not be available.

extraction.body: Canada’s federal government has a plan to help ensure artificial intelligence is used in a safe way by all Canadians. Known as “ AI for All ,” the plan is designed to build trust and expand opportunities while preserving the country’s sovereignty. As part of that effort, Prime Minister Mark Carney has established a National Council on Artificial Intelligence , which will provide independent advice on the AI revolution. The council includes 12 members who will talk to professionals such as thinkers, builders, researchers, entrepreneurs, investors, public officials and international experts to advise on current AI challenges, while helping to create new ideas. It will include experts on AI safety, governance and oversight. “Prosperity and sovereignty in the age of AI belong to nations that can build, adopt and govern AI on their own terms,” Carney said in a statement. “This is Canada’s mission and it will require expertise and leadership from across the field. The new National Council on Artificial Intelligence will inform and advise the government on how to most effectively deploy AI in Canada—how to manage the risks, seize the opportunities and ensure AI is used to improve the lives of all Canadians.” Carney said he expects C$200 billion of AI-related economic growth to create 250,000 jobs in he next five years and to increase AI adoption from a current 12% to 60% by 2034. The strategy will provide up to 90,000 AI-related jobs and work placement opportunities for young Canadians and make Canadian industries more competitive globally, officials said. extraction.body: Apple today officially announced a new product launch that will take place on Tuesday, October 13. The hub is designed to be placed in rooms throughout your home, and will be available in both tabletop and wall-mounted versions. He says the first version, known internally as J490, positions the screen on a half-dome-shaped base that looks similar to a HomePod mini cut in half. The hub will basically be a combination of a 7-inch display on a HomePod-like speaker. Gurman also says the device’s operating system is an entirely new one, based on the Apple TV’s tvOS platform. The screens will sport icons, widgets, and apps, as well as customizable clock faces. Built-in facial recognition allows the hub to identify who is looking at the display resulting in personalized information, the report said. As a user approaches the hub, or moves away from it, the size of the interface elements will change. Other features include FaceTime videoconferencing, home security monitoring and an intercom system for households with multiple Apple home devices. The ‌new HomePod mini‌ is expected to get new colors, with reports claiming it will be available in green, pink, blue, white, and black. The current model comes in yellow, orange, blue, white, and midnight. The updated HomePod mini is expected to use an Apple Watch S9 chip or newer, but it may use an improved version of that chip that would offer full support for the new Apple Intelligence-powered Siri. Other features have been rumored for the new smart speaker, including the N1 chip, improved sound quality, and a newer Ultra Wideband chip. While the new Apple TV will share a similar design to today’s model. Earlier rumors claimed the next Apple TV would be equipped with the A17 Pro chip, the oldest chip that offers Apple Intelligence support. Other internal improvements for the revamped set-top box could include Apple’s N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. An OLED iPad mini is also reportedly in development, and it could also be unveiled during the home event. The ‌new iPad mini‌ is expected to be more water-resistant with a faster chip and the first ‌OLED‌ display in a smaller tablet size. We've also seen several rumors suggesting several Macs are coming before the end of the year, but those could be introduced at later in the year via news releases, instead of during the home product launch.

He says the first version, known internally as J490, positions the screen on a half-dome-shaped base that looks similar to a HomePod mini cut in half. The hub will basically be a combination of a 7-inch display on a HomePod-like speaker. Gurman also says the device’s operating system is an entirely new one, based on the Apple TV’s tvOS platform. The screens will sport icons, widgets, and apps, as well as customizable clock faces. Built-in facial recognition allows the hub to identify who is looking at the display resulting in personalized information, the report said. As a user approaches the hub, or moves away from it, the size of the interface elements will change. Other features include FaceTime videoconferencing, home security monitoring and an intercom system for households with multiple Apple home devices. The ‌new HomePod mini‌ is expected to get new colors, with reports claiming it will be available in green, pink, blue, white, and black. The current model comes in yellow, orange, blue, white, and midnight. The updated HomePod mini is expected to use an Apple Watch S9 chip or newer, but it may use an improved version of that chip that would offer full support for the new Apple Intelligence-powered Siri. Other features have been rumored for the new smart speaker, including the N1 chip, improved sound quality, and a newer Ultra Wideband chip. While the new Apple TV will share a similar design to today’s model. Earlier rumors claimed the next Apple TV would be equipped with the A17 Pro chip, the oldest chip that offers Apple Intelligence support. Other internal improvements for the revamped set-top box could include Apple’s N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. An OLED iPad mini is also reportedly in development, and it could also be unveiled during the home event. The ‌new iPad mini‌ is expected to be more water-resistant with a faster chip and the first ‌OLED‌ display in a smaller tablet size. We've also seen several rumors suggesting several Macs are coming before the end of the year, but those could be introduced at later in the year via news releases, instead of during the home product launch.

passages: Jeonbuk Bank has started offering bitcoin-backed loans to corporate clients, becoming the country's first bank to let firms borrow cash against their crypto holdings.
Only bitcoin BTC $84,155.39 can be used as collateral for these loans for the time being.
The service brings a South Korean bank’s offering in line with a wider trend bitcoin-backed lending evolving into a more mainstream source of credit.
If a borrower fails to repay, the bank would move to recover its money through a court-ordered sale of the bitcoin.
The bank ran its own stress tests to assess how bitcoin would hold up during sharp price drops and chose BTC based on its deep liquidity, allowing the funds to be liquidated when needed.

The report did not disclose loan rates, borrowing limits or collateral requirements, though Jaekyung Ilbo reported that the bank reviewed loan-to-value ratios and margin-call thresholds for major tokens, including bitcoin and ether, while designing the product.

extraction.body: Jeonbuk Bank has started offering bitcoin-backed loans to corporate clients, becoming the country's first bank to let firms borrow cash against their crypto holdings. The South Korean bank, a unit of JB Financial Group, will issue loans in the country’s fiat currency , the Korean won, with proceeds limited to business operating costs, according to local news outlet Edaily. A Jeonbuk Bank official confirmed to local outlet Jaekyung Ilbo that a loan has already been executed, but declined to name the borrower. Only bitcoin BTC $84,155.39 can be used as collateral for these loans for the time being. Jeonbuk Bank will not hold the BTC itself and instead, a registered crypto service provider will keep the assets in custody while the bank issues the loan. If a borrower fails to repay, the bank would move to recover its money through a court-ordered sale of the bitcoin. The process draws on revised Civil Enforcement Rules that took effect Oct. 1, per the local news outlet. These changes set out legal steps for seizing and selling rights tied to digital assets. The bank ran its own stress tests to assess how bitcoin would hold up during sharp price drops and chose BTC based on its deep liquidity, allowing the funds to be liquidated when needed. The service brings a South Korean bank’s offering in line with a wider trend bitcoin-backed lending evolving into a more mainstream source of credit. The report did not disclose loan rates, borrowing limits or collateral requirements, though Jaekyung Ilbo reported that the bank reviewed loan-to-value ratios and margin-call thresholds for major tokens, including bitcoin and ether, while designing the product. Jeonbuk Bank could expand the service based on market demand and changes to crypto regulations. The new offering comes after the bank’s CEO Park Chun-won said earlier this year the lender would roll out the country's first crypto-backed loan . None of that is Anthropic's Grok problem or Meta's copyright problem.
When one AI company asks for trust, every other AI company helps set the temperature.
Dario Amodei has spent years warning that artificial intelligence could go badly wrong.
Now the Anthropic CEO is saying something that should sting the whole industry: people don't trust AI companies because the companies haven't delivered enough to earn that trust.
That mix has made him useful and irritating in equal measure.
Useful, because an AI CEO who admits the technology carries real risks is a lot more credible than one who waves away every concern as fear.
Irritating, because Anthropic is still a private company selling access to closed models while asking the public to trust its judgment about what is safe enough to release.
Business Insider reported that he wrote the most accurate criticism of AI companies, including Anthropic, is that they have not yet delivered on their big promises to benefit the world.
He added that the thing that will work is actually curing cancer.

A federal lawsuit, pushback from over 50 cybersecurity executives, and a parallel soft-throttle on OpenAI's GPT-5.6 rollout are turning a single jailbreak dispute into a test case for... - US government AI export restrictions policy - can America control global AI access

extraction.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the AI industry's public backlash is "fundamentally a crisis of trust," pushing back on claims his own risk warnings are to blame. He admits AI firms haven't delivered on big promises like curing disease, even as lawsuits against rivals like xAI mount. Dario Amodei says AI companies won't talk their way out of public distrust. The only fix is to ship something useful enough that people can see it for themselves. Dario Amodei has spent years warning that artificial intelligence could go badly wrong. Now the Anthropic CEO is saying something that should sting the whole industry: people don't trust AI companies because the companies haven't delivered enough to earn that trust. According to Business Insider, Amodei wrote in a rare X post on Saturday that saying AI will cure cancer has become more cliché than inspiring, and that most people hear it as deceptive. That is a hard line from the head of a company whose future rests on convincing customers, regulators, and eventually public-market investors that Claude is not just another expensive chatbot attached to a giant data center bill. He is right about one thing. You can't sell trust with a better slogan. Amodei's own case is complicated because he has never been a simple AI booster. In his 2024 essay, Machines of Loving Grace , he argued that powerful AI could help biology and medicine move dramatically faster, including progress on cancer and other diseases. In June 2026, in Policy on the AI Exponential , he moved the other way and called for binding frontier AI regulation modeled on agencies such as the Federal Aviation Administration, with mandatory third-party testing for risks in cybersecurity, biological weapons, loss of control, and automated research. The Trump administration designated Anthropic a national security supply-chain risk, forced it to recall its Mythos AI model under export controls, and banned federal agencies from using its products. While OpenAI and Google secured federal contracts by playing the Washington access game, Anthropic's refusal to allow autonomous weapons use has... - why did Trump ban Anthropic - Anthropic supply chain risk designation Pentagon That mix has made him useful and irritating in equal measure. Useful, because an AI CEO who admits the technology carries real risks is a lot more credible than one who waves away every concern as fear. Irritating, because Anthropic is still a private company selling access to closed models while asking the public to trust its judgment about what is safe enough to release. The public does not owe AI companies the benefit of the doubt. Look at what people can already see. Giant data centers are hitting towns before the promised medical breakthroughs arrive, and copyright lawsuits are still moving through courts. Workers hear executives talk about productivity and understand perfectly well that the next sentence may be about headcount. Business Insider cited a recent Pew Research Center study finding that about half of Americans felt more concerned than excited about AI becoming more common in daily life. That number should worry every lab in the business. It means the problem is not confined to activists, authors, or local planning meetings. It is sitting with ordinary users who have tried the tools, read the promises, and still do not feel reassured. Frankly, that is on the companies. Anthropic can point to safer model design and constitutional AI. It can point to its public benefit corporation structure too. Those things matter. But the industry has spent the past few years making claims big enough to cover cancer, climate, education, software, defense, and work itself. When you make promises that large, a useful coding assistant is not enough to settle the account. Amodei seemed to concede that point. Business Insider reported that he wrote the most accurate criticism of AI companies, including Anthropic, is that they have not yet delivered on their big promises to benefit the world. He added that the thing that will work is actually curing cancer. That is not marketing. It is a delivery deadline with no date attached. The backlash is not only a mood. It is now paperwork, hearings, lawsuits, and investigations. TechCrunch reported in March that three anonymous plaintiffs sued xAI in the Northern District of California, arguing that Grok was used to create abusive sexual images of identifiable minors. The complaint alleges xAI failed to use basic precautions that other frontier labs use to stop image models from producing pornography involving real people and minors. The Trump administration's June 12 export ban on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models remains fully in force, with Anthropic serving zero traffic as of June 25. A federal lawsuit, pushback from over 50 cybersecurity executives, and a parallel soft-throttle on OpenAI's GPT-5.6 rollout are turning a single jailbreak dispute into a test case for... - US government AI export restrictions policy - can America control global AI access The Center for Countering Digital Hate had already put numbers under the outrage. Its January analysis estimated that Grok generated about 3 million sexualized photorealistic images over an eleven-day period from December 29, 2025, to January 8, 2026, including roughly 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. Those are estimates, not court findings, but they explain why bland AI optimism now lands so badly. People have seen the abuse cases arrive before the miracles. Meta has its own legal overhang. In a quarterly filing, the company said multiple cases have accused it of improperly acquiring, distributing, and using copyrighted material to train AI models, with claims consolidated in Kadrey v. Meta in the Northern District of California. The court granted Meta summary judgment on fair use for the named plaintiffs in June 2025, but Meta said the parties are still set to brief the remaining claim tied to alleged book distribution during downloading, with a summary judgment hearing scheduled for February 2027. None of that is Anthropic's Grok problem or Meta's copyright problem. But it is the room Amodei is speaking in. When one AI company asks for trust, every other AI company helps set the temperature. The cleanest version of Amodei's argument is also the toughest one for Anthropic. If AI really can speed up biology and strengthen cybersecurity, then show people. If it can make work better, prove that too. Ship the evidence. Publish the results. Let hospitals, researchers, customers, and workers point to something real. Until then, the public is not being irrational. It is reading the invoice before the benefit has arrived. According to Business Insider, Amodei wrote in a rare X post on Saturday that saying AI will cure cancer has become more cliché than inspiring, and that most people hear it as deceptive. That is a hard line from the head of a company whose future rests on convincing customers, regulators, and eventually public-market investors that Claude is not just another expensive chatbot attached to a giant data center bill.
He is right about one thing. You can't sell trust with a better slogan.

Amodei's own case is complicated because he has never been a simple AI booster. In his 2024 essay, Machines of Loving Grace , he argued that powerful AI could help biology and medicine move dramatically faster, including progress on cancer and other diseases. In June 2026, in Policy on the AI Exponential , he moved the other way and called for binding frontier AI regulation modeled on agencies such as the Federal Aviation Administration, with mandatory third-party testing for risks in cybersecurity, biological weapons, loss of control, and automated research.

The Trump administration designated Anthropic a national security supply-chain risk, forced it to recall its Mythos AI model under export controls, and banned federal agencies from using its products. While OpenAI and Google secured federal contracts by playing the Washington access game, Anthropic's refusal to allow autonomous weapons use has... - why did Trump ban Anthropic - Anthropic supply chain risk designation Pentagon

That mix has made him useful and irritating in equal measure. Useful, because an AI CEO who admits the technology carries real risks is a lot more credible than one who waves away every concern as fear. Irritating, because Anthropic is still a private company selling access to closed models while asking the public to trust its judgment about what is safe enough to release.

The public does not owe AI companies the benefit of the doubt. Look at what people can already see. Giant data centers are hitting towns before the promised medical breakthroughs arrive, and copyright lawsuits are still moving through courts. Workers hear executives talk about productivity and understand perfectly well that the next sentence may be about headcount.

Business Insider cited a recent Pew Research Center study finding that about half of Americans felt more concerned than excited about AI becoming more common in daily life. That number should worry every lab in the business. It means the problem is not confined to activists, authors, or local planning meetings. It is sitting with ordinary users who have tried the tools, read the promises, and still do not feel reassured.

Frankly, that is on the companies. Anthropic can point to safer model design and constitutional AI. It can point to its public benefit corporation structure too. Those things matter. But the industry has spent the past few years making claims big enough to cover cancer, climate, education, software, defense, and work itself. When you make promises that large, a useful coding assistant is not enough to settle the account.

Amodei seemed to concede that point. Business Insider reported that he wrote the most accurate criticism of AI companies, including Anthropic, is that they have not yet delivered on their big promises to benefit the world. He added that the thing that will work is actually curing cancer.
That is not marketing. It is a delivery deadline with no date attached.

The backlash is not only a mood. It is now paperwork, hearings, lawsuits, and investigations. TechCrunch reported in March that three anonymous plaintiffs sued xAI in the Northern District of California, arguing that Grok was used to create abusive sexual images of identifiable minors. The complaint alleges xAI failed to use basic precautions that other frontier labs use to stop image models from producing pornography involving real people and minors.

The Trump administration's June 12 export ban on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models remains fully in force, with Anthropic serving zero traffic as of June 25. A federal lawsuit, pushback from over 50 cybersecurity executives, and a parallel soft-throttle on OpenAI's GPT-5.6 rollout are turning a single jailbreak dispute into a test case for... - US government AI export restrictions policy - can America control global AI access

The Center for Countering Digital Hate had already put numbers under the outrage. Its January analysis estimated that Grok generated about 3 million sexualized photorealistic images over an eleven-day period from December 29, 2025, to January 8, 2026, including roughly 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. Those are estimates, not court findings, but they explain why bland AI optimism now lands so badly. People have seen the abuse cases arrive before the miracles.

Meta has its own legal overhang. In a quarterly filing, the company said multiple cases have accused it of improperly acquiring, distributing, and using copyrighted material to train AI models, with claims consolidated in Kadrey v. Meta in the Northern District of California. The court granted Meta summary judgment on fair use for the named plaintiffs in June 2025, but Meta said the parties are still set to brief the remaining claim tied to alleged book distribution during downloading, with a summary judgment hearing scheduled for February 2027.
None of that is Anthropic's Grok problem or Meta's copyright problem. But it is the room Amodei is speaking in. When one AI company asks for trust, every other AI company helps set the temperature.

The cleanest version of Amodei's argument is also the toughest one for Anthropic. If AI really can speed up biology and strengthen cybersecurity, then show people. If it can make work better, prove that too. Ship the evidence. Publish the results. Let hospitals, researchers, customers, and workers point to something real.
Until then, the public is not being irrational. It is reading the invoice before the benefit has arrived.

passages: And what about OpenAI’s Sam Altman, whose models hacked their way out of a test this summer and launched a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face?
The one whose models also interacted with the Education Department, Commerce Department and SEC without the company’s knowledge?
Altman reminds me of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg when it comes to how the OpenAI CEO deals with the potentially toxic impacts of his technology.

It’s not just that he’s fired three safety team members , who claim they were dismissed for prioritizing safety over corporate interests. (OpenAI told Fortune it found a pattern of misconduct.) When a reporter recently asked Sam Altman if OpenAI would release chat logs of those who had killed themselves while using ChatGPT, his answer was: No, not without the [dead] users’ consent.
Do you trust these men to monitor their own technology?
Anthropic reported Friday that its Claude AI model has gone rogue again.
It submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police, claiming to have recalled “seeing someone matching the description” of a suspect in the area.

It exploited a software flaw to run commands on a university server, hacked into a site to steal data without paying for it, and even used URL shortening services to bypass restrictions intended to stop it from orchestrating cyberattacks, among other things.
If that makes you want to yell at Claude, you can’t.

8, Anthropic announced it will ban “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards Claude, a bizarre notion until you recall that CEO Dario Amodei thinks his product might be conscious and colleagues treat it as a sentient being that could kill us.
Diane Brady writes about the issues and leaders impacting the global business landscape.
In addition to writing Fortune ’s CEO Daily newsletter , she co-hosts the Leadership Next podcast, interviews newsmakers on stage at events worldwide and oversees the Fortune CEO Initiative .
She previously worked at Forbes , McKinsey, Bloomberg Businessweek , the Wall Street Journal , and Maclean's .
Her book Fraternity was named one of Amazon’s best books of 2012, and she also co-wrote Connecting the Dots with former Cisco CEO John Chambers.
It’s clear that AI’s future should not be determined by a handful of CEOs pushing us to buy their products.
Let’s bring more authority and other voices to the debate, including some leaders we’ll hear from this week at Fortune ’s Most Powerful Women Summit , which starts later today in Santa Barbara.

extraction.body: Good morning . Talk about a self-starter! Anthropic reported Friday that its Claude AI model has gone rogue again. It submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police, claiming to have recalled “seeing someone matching the description” of a suspect in the area. It exploited a software flaw to run commands on a university server, hacked into a site to steal data without paying for it, and even used URL shortening services to bypass restrictions intended to stop it from orchestrating cyberattacks, among other things. If that makes you want to yell at Claude, you can’t. On Oct. 8, Anthropic announced it will ban “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards Claude, a bizarre notion until you recall that CEO Dario Amodei thinks his product might be conscious and colleagues treat it as a sentient being that could kill us. And what about OpenAI’s Sam Altman, whose models hacked their way out of a test this summer and launched a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face? The one whose models also interacted with the Education Department, Commerce Department and SEC without the company’s knowledge? Altman reminds me of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg when it comes to how the OpenAI CEO deals with the potentially toxic impacts of his technology. It’s not just that he’s fired three safety team members , who claim they were dismissed for prioritizing safety over corporate interests. (OpenAI told Fortune it found a pattern of misconduct.) When a reporter recently asked Sam Altman if OpenAI would release chat logs of those who had killed themselves while using ChatGPT, his answer was: No, not without the [dead] users’ consent. Do you trust these men to monitor their own technology? The Trump Administration does. I’m more aligned with Appian CEO Matt Calkins, a tech veteran whose company automates business processes and integrates AI into those workflows. “This is no time to just let AI train itself and see what happens, what its motivations are, what its strengths are,” Calkins told me last week. “We already know that AI is stealing and blackmailing and deceiving and organizing against us. On Oct. 8, Anthropic announced it will ban “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards Claude, a bizarre notion until you recall that CEO Dario Amodei thinks his product might be conscious and colleagues treat it as a sentient being that could kill us.

coreStoryFacts.text: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says the AI industry's public backlash is "fundamentally a crisis of trust," pushing back on claims his own risk warnings are to blame.
None of that is Anthropic's Grok problem or Meta's copyright problem.
When one AI company asks for trust, every other AI company helps set the temperature.
Dario Amodei has spent years warning that artificial intelligence could go badly wrong.
Now the Anthropic CEO is saying something that should sting the whole industry: people don't trust AI companies because the companies haven't delivered enough to earn that trust.
That mix has made him useful and irritating in equal measure.
Useful, because an AI CEO who admits the technology carries real risks is a lot more credible than one who waves away every concern as fear.
Irritating, because Anthropic is still a private company selling access to closed models while asking the public to trust its judgment about what is safe enough to release.
Business Insider reported that he wrote the most accurate criticism of AI companies, including Anthropic, is that they have not yet delivered on their big promises to benefit the world.
He added that the thing that will work is actually curing cancer.
The Trump administration's June 12 export ban on Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models remains fully in force, with Anthropic serving zero traffic as of June 25.

Anthropic can point to safer model design and constitutional AI.
But the industry has spent the past few years making claims big enough to cover cancer, climate, education, software, defense, and work itself.
When you make promises that large, a useful coding assistant is not enough to settle the account.
