passages: And what about OpenAI’s Sam Altman, whose models hacked their way out of a test this summer and launched a cyberattack against the AI company Hugging Face?
The one whose models also interacted with the Education Department, Commerce Department and SEC without the company’s knowledge?
Altman reminds me of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg when it comes to how the OpenAI CEO deals with the potentially toxic impacts of his technology.

It’s not just that he’s fired three safety team members , who claim they were dismissed for prioritizing safety over corporate interests. (OpenAI told Fortune it found a pattern of misconduct.) When a reporter recently asked Sam Altman if OpenAI would release chat logs of those who had killed themselves while using ChatGPT, his answer was: No, not without the [dead] users’ consent.
Do you trust these men to monitor their own technology?
Anthropic reported Friday that its Claude AI model has gone rogue again.
It submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police, claiming to have recalled “seeing someone matching the description” of a suspect in the area.

It exploited a software flaw to run commands on a university server, hacked into a site to steal data without paying for it, and even used URL shortening services to bypass restrictions intended to stop it from orchestrating cyberattacks, among other things.
If that makes you want to yell at Claude, you can’t.

8, Anthropic announced it will ban “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” towards Claude, a bizarre notion until you recall that CEO Dario Amodei thinks his product might be conscious and colleagues treat it as a sentient being that could kill us.

passages: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has staunchly defended a controversial Pentagon plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting.

The proposal to publicly broadcast the military execution by firing squad has ignited intense debate over the morality of public capital punishment and the potential security risks associated with broadcasting the death of a convicted terrorist.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the livestreaming initiative last week, framing it as a necessary demonstration of absolute justice.

Despite warnings from lawmakers and human rights organizations that the broadcast could turn Hasan into a martyr, administration officials remain resolute in their commitment to making the execution a public spectacle.
Addressing the ethical objections raised by the media and civil liberties groups, the Homeland Security chief offered a blunt assessment: "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to."

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina echoed these sentiments, calling the plan "beyond disgusting" and warning that public executions are the hallmark of oppressive regimes like those in Iran and Afghanistan.
Several prominent conservative lawmakers have publicly condemned the livestreaming plan, arguing that it degrades the American justice system and elevates the status of a mass murderer.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended a controversial Pentagon plan to livestream the military execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has staunchly defended a controversial Pentagon plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting. The proposal to publicly broadcast the military execution by firing squad has ignited intense debate over the morality of public capital punishment and the potential security risks associated with broadcasting the death of a convicted terrorist. Hasan is scheduled to be executed on December 3, 2026, marking the first time the United States military has carried out a death sentence since 1961. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the livestreaming initiative last week, framing it as a necessary demonstration of absolute justice. Despite warnings from lawmakers and human rights organizations that the broadcast could turn Hasan into a martyr, administration officials remain resolute in their commitment to making the execution a public spectacle. During an appearance on CBS News' Face the Nation on Sunday, Secretary Mullin dismissed concerns regarding the potential for violent reprisals or extremist propaganda. When questioned about the elevated security risks of a global broadcast, Mullin argued that the spectacle serves as a critical deterrent. "I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime," Mullin stated. Addressing the ethical objections raised by the media and civil liberties groups, the Homeland Security chief offered a blunt assessment: "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to." Mullin emphasized his complete alignment with the administration's broader vision of executive authority and justice. "I follow President Trump. He's the commander in chief of the country... and he's restoring America's values," Mullin explained. He further noted that he harbored absolutely zero sympathy for Hasan, describing the perpetrator in harsh terms and stating he gives no thought to the manner in which the condemned man dies. The Pentagon's unprecedented decision has not been universally embraced within the Republican party. Several prominent conservative lawmakers have publicly condemned the livestreaming plan, arguing that it degrades the American justice system and elevates the status of a mass murderer. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska urged the Department of Defense to reverse what she termed a "gruesome decision." In a public statement, Murkowski declared, "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America. It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks." Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina echoed these sentiments, calling the plan "beyond disgusting" and warning that public executions are the hallmark of oppressive regimes like those in Iran and Afghanistan. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3. But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.” Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution. The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure. Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”. In a public statement, Murkowski declared, "I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America. It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks."

Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina echoed these sentiments, calling the plan "beyond disgusting" and warning that public executions are the hallmark of oppressive regimes like those in Iran and Afghanistan. The internal party friction was further complicated when Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on the necessity of the broadcast, noting that he personally would not tune in to watch the firing squad, despite acknowledging the severity of Hasan's crimes.

The execution of Nidal Hasan carries profound historical weight. In November 2009, Hasan opened fire at the Fort Hood Army Base in Texas, killing 13 unarmed soldiers and civilians while wounding over 30 others. He was subsequently convicted of premeditated murder and sentenced to death by a military jury. The case has spent over a decade winding through the military appellate courts.

If the December 3 execution proceeds as planned, it will end a 65-year hiatus on military capital punishment; the last military execution was the hanging of Army Private John A. Bennett in 1961. The utilization of a firing squad, combined with a global livestream, represents a radical departure from modern American penal norms.

International observers have also weighed in on the controversy. The United Nations human rights office issued a statement warning that broadcasting the execution would be "tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture." However, domestic proponents argue that the unique severity of an insider attack on a military installation warrants an equally exceptional public reckoning.

As the December execution date approaches, the Department of Homeland Security maintains that it is prepared for any potential domestic security fallout. Ultimately, the decision rests with the commander in chief, leaving the nation to grapple with the profound legal and moral implications of returning public executions to the digital age.

extraction.body: The decision to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution has triggered harsh criticism and warnings that it could encourage radicalisation. United States Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the planned livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution, playing down warnings that images of his death by firing squad might be used as a propaganda tool for violent groups. In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime. “I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”. Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US. “I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.” Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base. Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3. But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.” Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution. In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives. “Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said. “Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.” Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership. “It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said. The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure. Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”. She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution. “It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added. Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack. He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”. “Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X . “Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.” Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. If the order against Hasan is carried out, he will be the first member of the US military to be executed since 1961.

"Blockchains have finally found their raison d'être," the firm wrote. However, blockchain trading volumes do not necessarily represent the same type of activity as conventional securities markets. Citrini Research argues that Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create major investment opportunities without necessarily sending Bitcoin and Ethereum to new highs. "We can't assume that majors, primarily BTC and ETH, will make new ATHs on this," Citrini wrote, according to CoinDesk. "Even if they do, there are better expressions." Bitcoin's investment appeal remains closely tied to its role as a store of value and scarcity, while Ethereum provides infrastructure for smart contracts. However, Citrini argues that the biggest opportunities may lie with platforms that generate revenue as traditional financial assets move onto blockchain networks. Citrini's research examines a broader range of crypto projects positioned to benefit from tokenization. CCN has selected five cryptocurrencies from the projects discussed in coverage of Citrini's research, examining how each could benefit from Wall Street's blockchain expansion. Chainlink could play an important role in connecting traditional financial institutions with blockchain networks. Its infrastructure allows decentralized applications to access external information, including financial market data. That capability could become increasingly valuable if tokenized stocks and other securities begin moving between blockchain-based financial platforms. However, growing demand for Chainlink's services does not necessarily guarantee equivalent growth in LINK's market value. Ondo Finance represents one of the more direct connections between crypto and traditional financial markets. The company has developed products designed to provide blockchain-based exposure to conventional financial instruments, including US government securities. Its broader expansion into tokenized financial products places it within the market Citrini believes could grow substantially. There is also no guarantee that additional trading volume would directly increase UNI's value. Maple Finance focuses on blockchain-based lending and financial products, making it another potential beneficiary of institutional adoption. Unlike platforms primarily associated with retail crypto trading, Maple has developed services aimed at borrowers and investors seeking structured lending opportunities. Decentralized exchanges could generate substantial trading fees without necessarily distributing those earnings to token holders. Citrini's research suggests the next phase of blockchain adoption could look very different from previous crypto market cycles, with traditional financial assets and AI potentially driving demand . "The worlds of traditional finance and crypto are merging," the firm wrote. It argues that blockchain networks could increasingly support financial products used by mainstream institutions, while AI agents create demand for infrastructure that operates continuously. "AI agents move programmatically, 24/7, across applications," the report stated. For investors considering smaller cryptocurrencies, the challenge is determining whether the platforms benefiting from tokenization will deliver meaningful economic value to their token holders. Until a new source of sustained on-chain demand replaces what the meme coin season left behind, the developer numbers and the token price will keep pulling in opposite directions.

XRP at $7 turns $1,000 into $5,303. ETH at $10,000 makes it $4,970. SOL at $250 returns $3,041. BTC at $200,000 gives you $2,723. XRP has the highest ceiling by a significant margin, but it also has the most conditions attached to reaching it.

We think the right answer depends entirely on what you’re willing to hold through. Bitcoin gives $1,000 the most predictable outcome and the best-protected downside. XRP gives it the most upside if the legislative and macro catalysts align in the second half of 2026.

Wall Street's move onto blockchain could create a new generation of crypto winners, but Bitcoin and Ethereum may not capture the biggest gains. That's the investment thesis emerging from an Oct. 8 report by Citrini Research, which argues that the convergence of artificial intelligence and tokenized financial assets could transform global markets. However, that separation is now beginning to change. In its Oct. 8 report, Citrini points to the growing tokenization of traditional financial assets and the emergence of AI as two developments that could accelerate blockchain adoption. "Blockchains have finally found their raison d'être," the firm wrote. However, blockchain trading volumes do not necessarily represent the same type of activity as conventional securities markets. Citrini Research argues that Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create major investment opportunities without necessarily sending Bitcoin and Ethereum to new highs. "We can't assume that majors, primarily BTC and ETH, will make new ATHs on this," Citrini wrote, according to CoinDesk. "Even if they do, there are better expressions." Bitcoin's investment appeal remains closely tied to its role as a store of value and scarcity, while Ethereum provides infrastructure for smart contracts. However, Citrini argues that the biggest opportunities may lie with platforms that generate revenue as traditional financial assets move onto blockchain networks. Citrini's research examines a broader range of crypto projects positioned to benefit from tokenization. CCN has selected five cryptocurrencies from the projects discussed in coverage of Citrini's research, examining how each could benefit from Wall Street's blockchain expansion. Chainlink could play an important role in connecting traditional financial institutions with blockchain networks. Its infrastructure allows decentralized applications to access external information, including financial market data. That capability could become increasingly valuable if tokenized stocks and other securities begin moving between blockchain-based financial platforms. However, growing demand for Chainlink's services does not necessarily guarantee equivalent growth in LINK's market value. Ondo Finance represents one of the more direct connections between crypto and traditional financial markets. The company has developed products designed to provide blockchain-based exposure to conventional financial instruments, including US government securities. Its broader expansion into tokenized financial products places it within the market Citrini believes could grow substantially. There is also no guarantee that additional trading volume would directly increase UNI's value. Maple Finance focuses on blockchain-based lending and financial products, making it another potential beneficiary of institutional adoption. Unlike platforms primarily associated with retail crypto trading, Maple has developed services aimed at borrowers and investors seeking structured lending opportunities. Decentralized exchanges could generate substantial trading fees without necessarily distributing those earnings to token holders. Citrini's research suggests the next phase of blockchain adoption could look very different from previous crypto market cycles, with traditional financial assets and AI potentially driving demand . "The worlds of traditional finance and crypto are merging," the firm wrote. It argues that blockchain networks could increasingly support financial products used by mainstream institutions, while AI agents create demand for infrastructure that operates continuously. "AI agents move programmatically, 24/7, across applications," the report stated. For investors considering smaller cryptocurrencies, the challenge is determining whether the platforms benefiting from tokenization will deliver meaningful economic value to their token holders. Citrini's research suggests Wall Street's blockchain expansion could create a new generation of crypto winners. But as Ripple's expansion into Wall Street demonstrates, winning institutional business does not necessarily mean winning over cryptocurrency investors. Four of the most closely followed cryptos are all trading below their peaks right now. Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) has fallen below its October 2025 high, while Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) is 57% down from its all-time high. Meanwhile, XRP ( CRYPTO: XRP ) has been moving between $1.00 and $1.50 for months, and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) is 72% below its price in January 2025.

All four cryptocurrencies have specific reasons analysts expect them to move higher by the end of 2027, but the projected return on $1,000 varies enough between them to make this comparison genuinely worth running right now.

Today, Bitcoin is trading for $73,400, meaning $1,000 gets you around 0.0136 BTC. Bernstein has kept its $200,000 Bitcoin target for 2027 fixed even as Bitcoin has fallen 38% from its October 2025 high of $126,000. The firm’s analysts say the pullback doesn’t change the supply argument.

The April 2024 halving reduced annual Bitcoin production to 164,000 BTC, while institutional buying through ETFs and corporate treasuries is absorbing supply at a much faster rate than miners are producing. Spot Bitcoin ETFs have accumulated cumulative inflows of over $55 billion since their launch in January 2024, and Strategy holds more than 843,000 BTC on its balance sheet, having bought consistently through the 2026 drawdown.

Bitcoin has the lowest projected return of the four assets here at $1,000, but it’s also the most predictable route to reach the target and has the most institutional support behind it if macro conditions tighten. Standard Chartered is positioned slightly higher, with a $225,000 target in 2027. That $1,000 position is worth about $2,723 at a $200,000 target and $3,064 at $225,000.

The Ethereum network holds $45.5 billion in DeFi total value locked, more than any other blockchain. Tokenized US Treasury products on Ethereum hit $8 billion in May 2026, an all-time high after doubling in just six months. At the current price of $2,010 today, a $1,000 investment would buy roughly 0.498 ETH.

JPMorgan’s report on ETH in May 2026 says Ethereum has been losing ground to Bitcoin every week this year, and that the token is unlikely to turn that around unless on-chain activity picks up meaningfully and DeFi usage grows.

Standard Chartered analyst Geoff Kendrick reaffirmed his $10,000 ETH target by the end of 2027, with an $18,000 forecast for 2028. If the 2027 target is met, a $1,000 position would be worth around $4,970 at the current price of $2,010.

The CLARITY Act passed the Senate Banking Committee on May 14 in a bipartisan vote of 15-9 and now needs 60 votes on the full Senate floor before going to President Trump to be signed. The bill would permanently write XRP’s commodity classification into federal law, and that matters because the March 17 agency ruling that already granted XRP commodity status can be overturned by the next administration, while a law cannot.
Today, XRP is trading at $1.32, and $1,000 buys roughly 758 tokens. Standard Chartered is targeting $7 for XRP by the end of 2027, which would turn $1,000 invested today into around $5,303.

For that target to work, the CLARITY Act has to clear the full Senate, ETF inflows need to scale past $10 billion, and banks need to start settling directly in XRP rather than using stablecoins as a workaround on the ledger. Polymarket currently puts the odds of the bill passing in 2026 at 59%.

Solana added more than 11,500 new developers in the first nine months of 2025, second only to Ethereum globally, and had 2.2 million daily active wallets in Q1 2025 while keeping fees at around $0.00025 per transaction.

The Alpenglow upgrade targeted for 2026 would cut transaction confirmation from 12.8 seconds to around 150 milliseconds and give Solana the fastest confirmation time of any major Layer-1 network. At today’s price of $82, down 72% from its January 2025 peak of $294, $1,000 buys roughly 12.20 SOL.

Most analysts expect Solana to trade between $100 and $250 by 2027. At the high end of $250, a $1,000 position at today’s price grows to roughly $3,041. The main weight on the price is network revenue, which has dropped sharply since the meme coin boom that drove record activity in late 2024 ended.
Until a new source of sustained on-chain demand replaces what the meme coin season left behind, the developer numbers and the token price will keep pulling in opposite directions.

XRP at $7 turns $1,000 into $5,303. ETH at $10,000 makes it $4,970. SOL at $250 returns $3,041. BTC at $200,000 gives you $2,723. XRP has the highest ceiling by a significant margin, but it also has the most conditions attached to reaching it.

We think the right answer depends entirely on what you’re willing to hold through. Bitcoin gives $1,000 the most predictable outcome and the best-protected downside. XRP gives it the most upside if the legislative and macro catalysts align in the second half of 2026.

Ethereum is the bet on whether Glamsterdam and the next round of upgrades can finally pull on-chain activity back, because that’s the only thing that lets ETH outperform Bitcoin again. If they don’t, ETH keeps lagging the way it has since 2023.

Solana’s argument is that developer activity eventually translates into network revenue, but it hasn’t happened since the memecoin season ended. Which one gets your $1,000 depends on which risk you’re most comfortable taking.

passages: Shares of Michael Saylor-backed Strategy (MSTR) edged higher in pre-market trade on Monday as Bitcoin (BTC) tried to hold above $83,000, after the company announced the smallest BTC purchase of the year.
In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Strategy said that it had bought 250 BTC over the past week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin.
This is the smallest Bitcoin purchase the firm has made in 2026 and the 14th-smallest overall in its history as a Bitcoin treasury.
To fund its Bitcoin purchase, Strategy sold 125,183 MSTR shares for approximately $21 million.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

Nvidia has been a major contributor to the success of Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU). Unprecedented demand for Nvidia's GPUs has fueled equally impressive demand for Micron's high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM, and NAND processors, as the company is a major chip supplier to Nvidia. However, a persistent shortage of these data center memory chips -- which play a crucial role in AI processing -- may be working against Micron. For its flagship Vera Rubin chip, scheduled for release in the second half of 2026, Nvidia is reportedly using memory chips from Micron's biggest competitors. Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue » Reports out this morning suggest that SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics (OTC: SSNLF) will be the sole suppliers of sixth-generation HBM4 for the Vera Rubin processor, according to an article that first appeared in The Korea Economic Daily. The publication cited sources that suggest SK Hynix will supply more than half of Nvidia's total HBM supply this year, while Samsung will be the leading supplier of HBM4 chips for the Vera Rubin. SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics are the world's largest suppliers of HBM, with 34% and 33% of the market, respectively, according to Counterpoint Research. Micron controls 26% of the market, coming in third. This could have serious implications for Micron's future. The company's graphics processing units (GPUs) are at the heart of AI processing, and being a component supplier can have significant implications for a company's success or failure in AI.

Unprecedented demand for Nvidia's GPUs has fueled equally impressive demand for Micron's high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM, and NAND processors, as the company is a major chip supplier to Nvidia. However, a persistent shortage of these data center memory chips -- which play a crucial role in AI processing -- may be working against Micron. For its flagship Vera Rubin chip, scheduled for release in the second half of 2026, Nvidia is reportedly using memory chips from Micron's biggest competitors.

Will AI create the world's first trillionaire? Our team just released a report on the one little-known company, called an "Indispensable Monopoly" providing the critical technology Nvidia and Intel both need. Continue »

Reports out this morning suggest that SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics (OTC: SSNLF) will be the sole suppliers of sixth-generation HBM4 for the Vera Rubin processor, according to an article that first appeared in The Korea Economic Daily. The publication cited sources that suggest SK Hynix will supply more than half of Nvidia's total HBM supply this year, while Samsung will be the leading supplier of HBM4 chips for the Vera Rubin.

SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics are the world's largest suppliers of HBM, with 34% and 33% of the market, respectively, according to Counterpoint Research. Micron controls 26% of the market, coming in third.

This could have serious implications for Micron's future. Nvidia is the gold standard and market leader in data center GPUs, with an estimated 92% of the market, according to IoT Analytics. Furthermore, the biggest companies in technology -- namely Alphabet , Microsoft , Amazon , and Meta Platforms -- have announced plans to devote a combined $700 billion for capital expenditures in calendar 2026, with the vast majority of that spending earmarked for AI-centric data centers and servers.

However, the news isn't all bad. Citi analyst Atif Malik estimates that the cost of some memory chips will skyrocket 171% this year, fueled by persistent data center demand and the ongoing shortages. As a result, Micron likely won't have difficulty finding a market for its other memory chips, even those that Nvidia doesn't integrate into the Vera Rubin chip. Furthermore, Micron may be tapped later in the production cycle as shipments of Vera Rubin increase, according to Radio Free Mobile independent analyst Richard Windsor.

There's a bright side for investors. Like many stocks in the space, uncertainty has driven Micron down 13% from its peak, creating a rare opportunity to get it on sale. While Micron might not seem like a bargain at 36 times earnings, it has a much more reasonable forward multiple of 11. That's not a bad price to pay for a company expected to grow its revenue by 109% this year, according to Wall Street.

extraction.body: Australia is a relatively small country by population, with just 28 million citizens. But it has become a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) data center projects because of its vast land mass and favorable political climate. In fact, an Australian company called Firmus built a data center in Melbourne that houses the largest cluster of Nvidia 's ( NVDA -0.83% ) Blackwell Ultra chips in the entire Southern Hemisphere. Last week, Firmus was on track for one of the biggest initial public offerings (IPOs) in the history of the Australian stock market, which would've raised approximately $5 billion (U.S. dollars) at a $30 billion valuation. The company was going to use the funds to build more data centers across Australasia in order to expand its customer base, which already includes OpenAI and Meta Platforms . However, Firmus pulled the plug on its IPO at the last minute due to a lack of investor demand, which suggests funding might be starting to dry up for the AI industry. Mounting losses at some of the world's largest AI labs are an increasing concern, and rising interest rates are giving many investors a risk-free alternative for their money. Here's why this development could have negative consequences for semiconductor suppliers like Nvidia and Micron Technology ( MU -4.14% ) . According to Nvidia, the top-five hyperscale companies (including Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet) are on track to spend around $800 billion on AI data center infrastructure in 2026 and could spend a further $1.3 trillion in 2027. As a result, demand currently outstrips supply for critical chips like the graphics processing units ( GPUs ) supplied by Nvidia and the accompanying high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supplied by Micron. Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet build this infrastructure to develop their own AI software, but they also rent computing capacity to other businesses via their respective cloud platforms . This practice has become very lucrative, and Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, and Alphabet's Google Cloud each delivered accelerating revenue growth in the quarter ended June 30. In theory, hyperscalers will continue building more infrastructure as long as they believe there is demand for computing capacity. But cracks are starting to form; to keep up with the soaring costs of chips and components, companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and even Microsoft have dramatically raised prices for using their AI models and software over the last few months. OpenAI , for instance, recently introduced a new $500-per-month subscription plan for uncapped use of its flagship models, representing a whopping 150% increase over its $200-per-month plan, which used to be its most expensive offering. A report by the Financial Times last Thursday suggests OpenAI's annualized revenue is now tracking at $50 billion, below the $70 billion previously reported by other outlets. That might be a sign customers are pulling back amid the price hikes. That isn't surprising, considering companies like Uber Technologies , Walmart , AT&T , and even Amazon have placed AI usage restrictions on their employees this year to prevent budget blowouts. In fact, a recent survey by UBS Group found that 60% of businesses are diverting some AI workloads to cheaper, more efficient models to reduce costs. These models typically consume less computing power than those from labs like OpenAI, which could result in lower demand for chips. Therefore, Firmus' withdrawn IPO is just one more sign that sentiment toward AI might be shifting, at least temporarily. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 29.1 as I write this (Oct. 9), which is less than half its 10-year average of 61.3. Micron stock is even cheaper. Its P/E ratio is just 13.9, a sizable discount to both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 23.3 and 34.6, respectively. With an uncertain demand outlook and more supply scheduled to come online over the next couple of years, it appears Wall Street is betting the data center memory boom will be short lived. So, what should investors do? Those who already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to hold on and take a wait-and-see approach. Over the next month, the hyperscalers will release their operating results for the quarter ended Sept. 30. If they announce a pullback in capital expenditures, a slowdown in semiconductor demand is almost certainly on the horizon, which might be a sign for investors to trim their positions. Investors who don't already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to wait on the sidelines. While they seem cheap at face value, the market is sending a clear message that perhaps these companies won't grow their earnings as fast as initially expected over the next couple of years. extraction.body: Australia is a relatively small country by population, with just 28 million citizens. But it has become a major hub for artificial intelligence (AI) data center projects because of its vast land mass and favorable political climate. In fact, an Australian company called Firmus built a data center in Melbourne that houses the largest cluster of Nvidia 's ( NVDA -0.83% ) Blackwell Ultra chips in the entire Southern Hemisphere. Last week, Firmus was on track for one of the biggest initial public offerings (IPOs) in the history of the Australian stock market, which would've raised approximately $5 billion (U.S. dollars) at a $30 billion valuation. The company was going to use the funds to build more data centers across Australasia in order to expand its customer base, which already includes OpenAI and Meta Platforms . However, Firmus pulled the plug on its IPO at the last minute due to a lack of investor demand, which suggests funding might be starting to dry up for the AI industry. Mounting losses at some of the world's largest AI labs are an increasing concern, and rising interest rates are giving many investors a risk-free alternative for their money. Here's why this development could have negative consequences for semiconductor suppliers like Nvidia and Micron Technology ( MU -4.14% ) . According to Nvidia, the top-five hyperscale companies (including Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet) are on track to spend around $800 billion on AI data center infrastructure in 2026 and could spend a further $1.3 trillion in 2027. As a result, demand currently outstrips supply for critical chips like the graphics processing units ( GPUs ) supplied by Nvidia and the accompanying high-bandwidth memory (HBM) supplied by Micron. Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet build this infrastructure to develop their own AI software, but they also rent computing capacity to other businesses via their respective cloud platforms . This practice has become very lucrative, and Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services, and Alphabet's Google Cloud each delivered accelerating revenue growth in the quarter ended June 30. In theory, hyperscalers will continue building more infrastructure as long as they believe there is demand for computing capacity. But cracks are starting to form; to keep up with the soaring costs of chips and components, companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and even Microsoft have dramatically raised prices for using their AI models and software over the last few months. OpenAI , for instance, recently introduced a new $500-per-month subscription plan for uncapped use of its flagship models, representing a whopping 150% increase over its $200-per-month plan, which used to be its most expensive offering. A report by the Financial Times last Thursday suggests OpenAI's annualized revenue is now tracking at $50 billion, below the $70 billion previously reported by other outlets. That might be a sign customers are pulling back amid the price hikes. That isn't surprising, considering companies like Uber Technologies , Walmart , AT&T , and even Amazon have placed AI usage restrictions on their employees this year to prevent budget blowouts. In fact, a recent survey by UBS Group found that 60% of businesses are diverting some AI workloads to cheaper, more efficient models to reduce costs. These models typically consume less computing power than those from labs like OpenAI, which could result in lower demand for chips. Therefore, Firmus' withdrawn IPO is just one more sign that sentiment toward AI might be shifting, at least temporarily. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 29.1 as I write this (Oct. 9), which is less than half its 10-year average of 61.3. Micron stock is even cheaper. Its P/E ratio is just 13.9, a sizable discount to both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 23.3 and 34.6, respectively. With an uncertain demand outlook and more supply scheduled to come online over the next couple of years, it appears Wall Street is betting the data center memory boom will be short lived. So, what should investors do? Those who already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to hold on and take a wait-and-see approach. Over the next month, the hyperscalers will release their operating results for the quarter ended Sept. 30. If they announce a pullback in capital expenditures, a slowdown in semiconductor demand is almost certainly on the horizon, which might be a sign for investors to trim their positions. Investors who don't already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to wait on the sidelines. While they seem cheap at face value, the market is sending a clear message that perhaps these companies won't grow their earnings as fast as initially expected over the next couple of years. That might be a sign customers are pulling back amid the price hikes.

That isn't surprising, considering companies like Uber Technologies , Walmart , AT&T , and even Amazon have placed AI usage restrictions on their employees this year to prevent budget blowouts. In fact, a recent survey by UBS Group found that 60% of businesses are diverting some AI workloads to cheaper, more efficient models to reduce costs. These models typically consume less computing power than those from labs like OpenAI, which could result in lower demand for chips.
Therefore, Firmus' withdrawn IPO is just one more sign that sentiment toward AI might be shifting, at least temporarily.
Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 29.1 as I write this (Oct. 9), which is less than half its 10-year average of 61.3.

Micron stock is even cheaper. Its P/E ratio is just 13.9, a sizable discount to both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes, which have P/E ratios of 23.3 and 34.6, respectively. With an uncertain demand outlook and more supply scheduled to come online over the next couple of years, it appears Wall Street is betting the data center memory boom will be short lived.

So, what should investors do? Those who already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to hold on and take a wait-and-see approach. Over the next month, the hyperscalers will release their operating results for the quarter ended Sept. 30. If they announce a pullback in capital expenditures, a slowdown in semiconductor demand is almost certainly on the horizon, which might be a sign for investors to trim their positions.

Investors who don't already own shares of Nvidia and Micron might want to wait on the sidelines. While they seem cheap at face value, the market is sending a clear message that perhaps these companies won't grow their earnings as fast as initially expected over the next couple of years.

In January 2023, Bitcoin climbed above the average near $23,000 and rose 217% to a high of around $73,000 by March 2024. Conversely, in April 2019, it rebounded to near $5,000 and initially surged 170% to about $13,800 by June, but then fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December of that same year.
So what does a fourth consecutive weekly close above the average suggest about what might happen next for Bitcoin holders?

The 50-week average is calculated by averaging Bitcoin’s closing prices for the past 50 weeks. It helps smooth out price fluctuations, giving a clearer picture of longer-term trends. When Bitcoin stays above this average, it indicates that buyers are dominating the market. If it trades below, it suggests sellers are in control.

The ‘weekly close’ refers to the last price at the end of each trading week. Traders typically regard this price as more significant than daily closes because it reduces market noise. Since Bitcoin is traded around the clock, a sudden price spike on a single day can briefly push the price above or below the average before reverting back. A weekly close counts only if Bitcoin is above the line when the week ends.

When Bitcoin achieves four consecutive weekly closes above this average, it sets a higher standard. A single close might be a temporary bounce, but four consecutive ones show buyers have consistently held the price up.

The 2023 signal is often touted as a success story. When Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week average near $23,000 in January 2023, it skyrocketed 217% to roughly $73,000 by March 2024. Those who interpreted this signal as the start of a new uptrend were vindicated.

In contrast, the 2019 signal began similarly. After regaining the average near $5,000 in April 2019, it rose to about $13,800 by June—a significant increase. However, this rally was short-lived: Bitcoin fell about 50% to about $6,500 by December, leaving those who held through the year disappointed.

Analysts attribute these differences to factors like liquidity, the amount of money flowing into riskier investments, and the timing of halving events, when the rate of new Bitcoin production is reduced. However, with only two instances to reference, these explanations remain speculative.

Bitcoin is currently about 33.9% below its record high of $126,080 . It has risen 8.0% over the past 30 days but fallen 3.2% in the last week. This mix of trends could indicate a scenario similar to either of the previous signals.

The 50-week average is always changing. Each week, the oldest closing price drops out of the calculation while the most recent price is included, slightly altering the average Bitcoin needs to maintain.

This four-week streak strongly suggests Bitcoin’s trend may be shifting upward. However, it doesn’t necessarily indicate how far the price will rise or how long this trend will last. Both past signals preceded significant gains, but one of those gains was largely lost by the year’s end.

For now, holders should pay close attention. A weekly close below the average, currently around $76,618, would end the streak and suggest a shift back towards a downtrend. Until then, either a repeat of the 2023 rally or a downturn like 2019 remains possible .

sources.title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia - CNBC
passages: Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice.
Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027.
The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.
Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation.
CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor.
And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.
Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie.
But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 .

It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients.
And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
"Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI trade

Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google . The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade." Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline. "We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said. Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs. "We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well." Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company. In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares. Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said. Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies. "Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy. passages: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is built around one question: How do you build an enduring company in the AI era?
Our programming and speaker lineup reflect that, based on the feedback we’ve gotten from the community and the reality on the ground.
And everything kicks off in just a few days, act now before your chance to save $100 on your pass comes to an end .
If you’re asking Claude or ChatGPT if TechCrunch Disrupt is worth it, you’re not alone.
The reality is that Disrupt is a unique event, and it’s happening at a unique time for the startup community.
This year’s Disrupt isn’t about predicting the future of AI; it’s about building companies in it.
Across six editorially curated stages, founders will hear practical lessons from the CEOs, investors, engineers, and operators shaping the next decade of technology.
That’s not the exception at Disrupt — that’s the point.
And those opportunities aren’t just available for Battlefield finalists.
Every conversation in the Expo Hall or in a Side Event can create an opportunity for your startup.
For years, whether it’s been held in New York, San Francisco, or elsewhere, Disrupt has brought together thousands of founders, investors, startup team members, and tech leaders.
Check out the full lineup of speakers across all stages and events here .
Prioritize our investor-matchmaking tools and the connections that come with your Founder Pass, including the networking tools in our app.
You also get access to the Deal Flow Café, where we foster one-on-one conversations between founders and investors.
Disrupt’s Side Events aren’t to be missed — there’s one for every industry, interest, or post-event vibe you could be looking to find.
The 200 startups chosen on August 20 to compete go through a rigorous prep process and get the opportunity to pitch onstage in front of top-tier VCs and the Disrupt crowds.
You’ll also get to watch those pitches, take notes, learn from the peaks and valleys, and potentially meet the teams behind the ideas and innovations.
It could be in a follow-up meeting or just walking through the halls of Moscone.
Last year at Disrupt, we spoke with founders about their experiences and discovered the results of their attendance firsthand.
And if that all leaves you inspired, here’s an insider tip: Most Battlefield participants, and several winners, have gone through the process multiple times.

If there are colleagues in your network who have been impacted by layoffs who you’d like to have join up, we have an option for them as well, with a special $75 Expo+ Pass available at a limited volume for those impacted by cutbacks this year .
But it’s the lead-up to that $100,000 check and the deluge of attention the winner receives that’s the most valuable for founders attending Disrupt.

Consider that every founder pitching during the Startup Battlefield competition does so in front of a packed room of VCs. Why? Because they know their next cohort could be sitting right there. All it takes is making the trip to San Francisco this October 13-15 . This guide is for the investors who recognize that three days spent at Moscone West are well worth it and who plan to walk away with the insights and prospects that yield returns. Disrupt features numerous tracks, depending on the check sizes you’re able to write and the stage of startup you specialize in. If you’re coming to build out your portfolio of early bets and get in on rounds before they’re priced, prioritize the Startup Battlefield 200 semifinalist pitches, the Builders Stage , and the Expo Hall . Disrupt will be all about volume and speed of qualified deal flow. Prioritize the founder list, our curated 1:1 meetings, and the Deal Flow Café. This stage is best suited for those coming to the event as much for market intelligence and strategic partnership scouting as for deal sourcing. Prioritize the Smart Money and Smart Systems Stages, as well as the exclusive StrictlyVC investor-only session. More than 20,000 curated meetings take place over just three days, within dedicated environments like investor receptions and structured networking sessions. Investor-founder connections aren’t hallway luck –they’re built into Disrupt’s infrastructure. You get direct access to 200 pitch-ready, TechCrunch-vetted startups through Startup Battlefield 200 . And we’ll put an emphasis on “vetted.” Our Startup Battlefield team, working alongside TechCrunch’s incredibly discerning team of editors and writers, has done a significant amount of diligence for you already. Past speakers have included investors like Elad Gil and Vinod Khosla, and this year’s lineup puts you in the room with the operators you’re underwriting, too. We’re talking Rivian’s RJ Scaringe, Amazon’s Panos Panay, Replit’s Amjad Masad, and Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, just for starters. The Disrupt crowd is your signal. With a mix of 10,000 founders, investors, and operators filling Moscone West, the companies worth knowing will get discovered by someone. This is your chance to make sure it’s you. For founders, Startup Battlefield is a visibility engine and a trial by fire. For investors, it’s a filtered shortlist that the TechCrunch team has spent months narrowing down for you. Startup Battlefield is intensely competitive. Thousands of global startups apply, while just 200 make the cut and only a handful reach the finals. That funnel is doing your top-of-pipeline filtering for you before you ever take a meeting. If you’re not circling around these startups, your competitors are. We have several different passes for Disrupt, and by joining the community via an Investor Pass, you get access to perks like… This is a space exclusively for founders and investors, fostering impromptu run-ins with founders actively seeking capital. Grab coffee or a beverage of choice, explore opportunities, and start conversations that can turn into your next deal. You’ll get early access to the full list of Disrupt founders looking for connections with investors. The next addition to your portfolio can be identified before the event even begins, giving you more time to find even more opportunities. Through the Disrupt app, you can schedule 1:1 and small-group meetings with founders matching your focus areas, with AI helping match you by mutual interests instead of waiting on fate. The investors who make the most out of Disrupt don’t leave sourcing to chance — they’ve already scanned the available resources and set up their agendas in advance. Our editorially curated programming, including all three days of sessions and panels, is available here , stretching across six stages, breakout sessions, roundtables, and Side Events. Here are some of the stages that might be of interest: The Smart Money Stage : Interested in capital markets, embedded finance, and stablecoins? Everything within the fintech realm, especially within the intersection of AI, is included. The Smart Systems Stage : It’s all about compute, infrastructure, and energy economics. If you need to build a justification for underwriting AI infrastructure bets, this is the place to start. The AI Stage and Real World AI Stages : Get market intelligence on where the fastest-growing startups are deploying, not just building. The Disrupt Stage : This is where operators and CEOs set the narrative your current and future portfolio companies will be measured against. We’ve gone in depth about the benefits to you, your portfolio, and the opportunities Disrupt offers you. But there are always matters of hotels, expenses, and travel to sort out. Our Disrupt site has the bulk of these issues covered, but to tackle some common questions and pressing opportunities: For your hotel needs , we have partnerships with several stellar hotels near Moscone West. You’ll get exclusive discounts, easy access to Disrupt and anything else you might want to explore in San Francisco, and yes, you’ll get points for your accommodations. If you’re bringing a large cohort or are interested in having a company in your portfolio take part in our Expo Hall to get wider visibility, check out our bulk ticket options here and our Exhibit Table options here . For all other questions, you can explore our full Disrupt page to find more specific FAQs, and we hope to see you in San Francisco this year! At Disrupt, the volume and competition are the point for investors, not a drawback. Year after year, investors who’ve explored the Expo Halls, met founders, and learned from peers at panels and Side Events have proven why you need to be on the ground to get ahead of the curve.

Consider that every founder pitching during the Startup Battlefield competition does so in front of a packed room of VCs. Why? Because they know their next cohort could be sitting right there. All it takes is making the trip to San Francisco this October 13-15 .
This guide is for the investors who recognize that three days spent at Moscone West are well worth it and who plan to walk away with the insights and prospects that yield returns.
Disrupt features numerous tracks, depending on the check sizes you’re able to write and the stage of startup you specialize in.

If you’re coming to build out your portfolio of early bets and get in on rounds before they’re priced, prioritize the Startup Battlefield 200 semifinalist pitches, the Builders Stage , and the Expo Hall .
Disrupt will be all about volume and speed of qualified deal flow. Prioritize the founder list, our curated 1:1 meetings, and the Deal Flow Café.

This stage is best suited for those coming to the event as much for market intelligence and strategic partnership scouting as for deal sourcing. Prioritize the Smart Money and Smart Systems Stages, as well as the exclusive StrictlyVC investor-only session.

More than 20,000 curated meetings take place over just three days, within dedicated environments like investor receptions and structured networking sessions. Investor-founder connections aren’t hallway luck –they’re built into Disrupt’s infrastructure.

You get direct access to 200 pitch-ready, TechCrunch-vetted startups through Startup Battlefield 200 . And we’ll put an emphasis on “vetted.” Our Startup Battlefield team, working alongside TechCrunch’s incredibly discerning team of editors and writers, has done a significant amount of diligence for you already.

Past speakers have included investors like Elad Gil and Vinod Khosla, and this year’s lineup puts you in the room with the operators you’re underwriting, too. We’re talking Rivian’s RJ Scaringe, Amazon’s Panos Panay, Replit’s Amjad Masad, and Cerebras’ Andrew Feldman, just for starters.

The Disrupt crowd is your signal. With a mix of 10,000 founders, investors, and operators filling Moscone West, the companies worth knowing will get discovered by someone. This is your chance to make sure it’s you.
For founders, Startup Battlefield is a visibility engine and a trial by fire. For investors, it’s a filtered shortlist that the TechCrunch team has spent months narrowing down for you.

Startup Battlefield is intensely competitive. Thousands of global startups apply, while just 200 make the cut and only a handful reach the finals. That funnel is doing your top-of-pipeline filtering for you before you ever take a meeting. If you’re not circling around these startups, your competitors are.
We have several different passes for Disrupt, and by joining the community via an Investor Pass, you get access to perks like…

This is a space exclusively for founders and investors, fostering impromptu run-ins with founders actively seeking capital. Grab coffee or a beverage of choice, explore opportunities, and start conversations that can turn into your next deal.

You’ll get early access to the full list of Disrupt founders looking for connections with investors. The next addition to your portfolio can be identified before the event even begins, giving you more time to find even more opportunities.
Through the Disrupt app, you can schedule 1:1 and small-group meetings with founders matching your focus areas, with AI helping match you by mutual interests instead of waiting on fate.
The investors who make the most out of Disrupt don’t leave sourcing to chance — they’ve already scanned the available resources and set up their agendas in advance.

Our editorially curated programming, including all three days of sessions and panels, is available here , stretching across six stages, breakout sessions, roundtables, and Side Events. Here are some of the stages that might be of interest:
The Smart Money Stage : Interested in capital markets, embedded finance, and stablecoins? Everything within the fintech realm, especially within the intersection of AI, is included.
The Smart Systems Stage : It’s all about compute, infrastructure, and energy economics. If you need to build a justification for underwriting AI infrastructure bets, this is the place to start.
The AI Stage and Real World AI Stages : Get market intelligence on where the fastest-growing startups are deploying, not just building.
The Disrupt Stage : This is where operators and CEOs set the narrative your current and future portfolio companies will be measured against.

We’ve gone in depth about the benefits to you, your portfolio, and the opportunities Disrupt offers you. But there are always matters of hotels, expenses, and travel to sort out. Our Disrupt site has the bulk of these issues covered, but to tackle some common questions and pressing opportunities:

For your hotel needs , we have partnerships with several stellar hotels near Moscone West. You’ll get exclusive discounts, easy access to Disrupt and anything else you might want to explore in San Francisco, and yes, you’ll get points for your accommodations.

If you’re bringing a large cohort or are interested in having a company in your portfolio take part in our Expo Hall to get wider visibility, check out our bulk ticket options here and our Exhibit Table options here .
For all other questions, you can explore our full Disrupt page to find more specific FAQs, and we hope to see you in San Francisco this year!

In the US, this would mean, for example, revisiting the National Emergencies Act and International Emergency Economic Powers Act, and closing the “data broker” loophole in intelligence work. As executive agencies begin to leverage AI, we should also furnish Congress and the courts with equally powerful AI tools, so that their oversight can keep pace. The principle here is not new. As James Madison wrote, “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition,” only here in a digital setting. Longer-term, to avoid widespread political disempowerment, we will need to renew our traditions of self-government, involving citizens more directly in policymaking and government oversight. If we play our cards right, AI itself may help, making information easier to access and helping citizens reason together – town halls for a digital age. Buttressing political freedom in these ways would be important in its own right. Today, however, it is also a form of AI safety work. Who is best positioned to drive the needed reforms? Policymakers, civic organizations and ordinary citizens must all participate. But there is another key player: the AI industry. While the major AI labs are willing to weigh in on specific policy issues, most have recently gone quiet on the topic of democracy itself. Over the past year, a number of AI-industry leaders have justifiably stressed the need to equip military and intelligence agencies with AI, so that democracies can compete abroad. In 2018, Microsoft publicly asked Congress to limit government use of facial recognition technology, writing: “We must ensure that the year 2024 doesn’t look like a page from the novel 1984 .” And as recently as 2021, companies including Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Facebook, IBM, Microsoft and Twitter published an open letter opposing proposed changes to state voting laws, declaring: “We stand for democracy.”

More recently, however, many tech companies have fallen silent. This is understandable. These companies answer to their investors, and in the current environment, speaking out can put shareholder value at risk.

That, however, should not be the end of the story. The leading AI labs all describe AI safety as core to their mission. If they mean what they say, then – for the reasons I’ve highlighted – they bear a duty to stand up for basic constitutional principles, despite the commercial risks.
Journalists, researchers and ordinary citizens can help them recognize that duty by insistently pointing out the connection between safety and freedom.
It is good that people outside the AI industry are suddenly talking about AI safety. AI will affect everyone, and everyone should be involved in shaping how it is built and used.

But we need to make political freedom a centerpiece of the discussion. We need to build public awareness that AI safety fundamentally depends on democracy. Only by bearing this point firmly in mind can we avoid the dangers of AI and reap its potentially immense benefits.

Matthew Botvinick is the author of the forthcoming book AI and Political Freedom and a senior fellow at Yale Law School. He has held multiple research positions in the AI industry, including at Google DeepMind and currently Anthropic, but writes here exclusively in his Yale role

sources.title: These execs think voice AI hasn’t reached its ChatGPT moment yet
passages: Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one.
However, in reality, that might not be the case.
Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet.

“If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it.
“For Otter, you know, transcription was never the end point.
It was just the layer that we could start to drive some of the productivity gains on the back of.
And the minute that starts to take action, that is wrong.
It is critical for us to continue to improve that ASR model because all of the downstream impacts are significant,” he said.
Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation.
The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings.
For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting.
He also said that language is one area where voice models need to improve.
With the new voice tools, there is also a question of transparency.
Tools should declare to customers that they are being recorded or talking to AI.

extraction.body: The theory of voice being the next big interface has picked up strong momentum, with investors pouring billions of dollars into voice AI startups working on areas ranging from model makers to enterprise customer service providers, and from meeting note-takers to AI-powered dictation. Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one. However, in reality, that might not be the case. Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet. “We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models. The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month. He also said that AI agents in customer service should not sound robotic and should give callers enough confidence that they can solve problems. “I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said. Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation. The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings. For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting. “If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it. If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a q and a chatbot,” Gay noted. While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting notetaker shows the wrong transcript or a summary. Wen thinks that ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition) models often miss important keywords, and that creates an issue in capturing the whole context. Otter’s Gay agreed with this, adding that the company keeps working on improving transcription. He also said that language is one area where voice models need to improve. “For Otter, you know, transcription was never the end point. It was just the layer that we could start to drive some of the productivity gains on the back of. But if your original transcription didn’t have the accuracy that you needed, all the follow-up actions that you have become flawed. And the minute that starts to take action, that is wrong. You lose trust in the platform. It is critical for us to continue to improve that ASR model because all of the downstream impacts are significant,” he said. With the new voice tools, there is also a question of transparency. Tools should declare to customers that they are being recorded or talking to AI. Otter said that it wants to instill trust in people who are in a meeting, so even for a meeting where the bot is not present, it wants to try methods like notifying everyone in the chat that the meeting is being recorded. PolyAI’s Wen also said that it’s important to establish that people are talking to an AI in enterprise calls.
